Compute Savings Plans
Standard Reserved Instances (RIs)
Convertible Reserved Instances (RIs)
items.exp: Compute Savings Plans provide up to 66% discount off On-Demand rates and automatically apply to usage across Amazon EC2 (any instance family, size, OS, or tenancy), AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda, as well as across any AWS Region.

items.q: A solo founder runs a SaaS telemetry platform on AWS consisting of 16 stateless Go and Python microservices in Docker containers on Amazon ECS (EC2 launch type using `m6i.xlarge`), two Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instances (`db.m6i.2xlarge`), and an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster (`cache.r6i.xlarge`). None of the workloads depend on x86-specific native binaries. What is the most straightforward architecture change to reduce compute costs by ~20% while improving price-performance by up to 40%?
opts: Migrate the PostgreSQL databases and Redis caches onto AWS Lambda functions.
Enable EBS Multi-Attach on all RDS and ElastiCache instances.

Build multi-architecture (`linux/arm64`) container images and migrate the EC2 fleet, RDS for PostgreSQL instances, and ElastiCache for Redis nodes to AWS Graviton3/Graviton4 (`m7g`/`r7g`) instance families.
Switch the VPC from IPv4 to IPv6.
items.exp: AWS Graviton (`arm64`) processors (`m7g`, `c7g`, `r7g`, `r8g`) deliver up to 40% better price-performance and ~20% lower hourly cost compared to comparable x86 (`i`/`a`) instances across Amazon EC2, Fargate, Lambda, RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache, and OpenSearch—requiring zero code changes for interpreted languages (Python/Node), Go multi-arch builds, and managed AWS databases.

items.q: Mammoth Capital ingests 600 million tiny JSON market-tick files per day into an Amazon S3 bucket. Because of regulatory mandates, the bucket uses Server-Side Encryption with AWS KMS Customer Managed Keys (SSE-KMS). At the end of the first month, the FinOps lead is shocked to see an AWS KMS bill of $54,000/month just for `GenerateDataKey` and `Decrypt` API calls (at $0.03 per 10,000 requests), far exceeding the actual S3 storage cost. Compliance still requires SSE-KMS with the Customer Managed Key and CloudTrail auditability. What single S3 configuration change can reduce the AWS KMS request cost by up to 99%?
opts: Switch the bucket encryption from SSE-KMS to SSE-S3 (AES-256).
Deploy an AWS CloudHSM cluster in front of Amazon S3.
Move all 600 million objects per day directly into S3 Glacier Deep Archive on PUT.
Enable S3 Bucket Keys on the S3 bucket.
items.exp: S3 Bucket Keys reduce AWS KMS API request costs by up to 99% by generating a short-lived bucket-level key from your KMS key and temporarily retaining it within S3 to mint individual object data keys locally inside S3, rather than calling KMS `GenerateDataKey`/`Decrypt` for every single S3 PUT/GET operation.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's Quantitative Research group stores 800 TB of alternative datasets (satellite imagery, shipping manifests, and earnings-call audio) in Amazon S3. Each dataset averages 250 MB per object. Some datasets are queried intensively for 3 weeks and then untouched for 8 months, while others are unexpectedly re-queried by new ML pipelines at unpredictable times. When a dataset is re-queried, researchers cannot tolerate per-GB retrieval fees, and for objects untouched for more than 90 or 180 days, they can wait 3–12 hours for asynchronous restoration if it saves an extra 68–95% on storage. Which S3 storage strategy is most cost-effective?
opts: Store all objects in S3 Standard-IA and use a Lambda function to copy objects back to S3 Standard when queried.
Store the objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering and activate the optional Archive Access (90 days) and Deep Archive Access (180 days) tiers.
Transition all objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 day using an S3 Lifecycle policy.
Store all objects in S3 One Zone-IA and disable S3 Versioning.
items.exp: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects ≥128 KB between Frequent Access, Infrequent Access (after 30 days), and Archive Instant Access (after 90 days) with zero retrieval fees when accessed, and optionally down to asynchronous Archive Access (90–270+ days) and Deep Archive Access (180–730+ days) for maximum long-term savings.

items.q: Mammoth Capital stores 2 PB of 7-year historical equities tick archives in Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Once per quarter, the Quantitative Strategy team needs to restore a 40 TB slice of 5-year-old archives into a temporary S3 Standard prefix to run a weekend backtest. The job is scheduled on Friday morning and does not start running until Friday night, so a retrieval completion time of 5 to 12 hours is completely acceptable. Which S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval option minimizes retrieval costs for this 40 TB restore?
opts: Expedited retrieval (1–5 minutes)
Standard retrieval (3–5 hours)
Provisioned Capacity units
Bulk retrieval (5–12 hours)
items.exp: In Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, Bulk retrievals complete within 5 to 12 hours and have the lowest cost—in fact, Bulk data retrievals (per-GB fee) in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval are free (you only pay a tiny per-1,000 request fee), saving thousands of dollars on a 40 TB restore compared to Standard ($0.01/GB = $400) or Expedited ($0.03/GB = $1,200).

items.q: Mammoth Capital runs a high-throughput Apache Kafka cluster and 30 consumer microservices across three Availability Zones (`us-east-1a`, `us-east-1b`, `us-east-1c`) inside a single VPC. Although all traffic stays on private RFC1918 IP addresses inside the VPC, their monthly AWS bill shows $38,000 in `EC2-Other` (`USE1-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes`) charges because consumers in `us-east-1a` are constantly fetching 1.9 PB/month of market streams from Kafka brokers in `us-east-1b` and `us-east-1c` (billed at $0.01/GB in each direction, or $0.02/GB round-trip across AZ boundaries). Resiliency across all three AZs must be maintained. How can the architect drastically cut this Regional Data Transfer bill without sacrificing Multi-AZ high availability?
opts: Route the traffic between the three Availability Zones through a centralized AWS Transit Gateway.
Enable VPC Peering between `us-east-1a` and `us-east-1b`.

Configure Availability Zone affinity (rack-aware consumer routing / Istio or ALB Target Group Availability Zone affinity / AZ-ID mapping) so that under normal healthy operations, consumers read from Kafka broker replicas located in the exact same Availability Zone (`use1-az1` to `use1-az1`), failing over across AZs only when an AZ is unhealthy.
Move the Kafka brokers onto public IPv4 addresses and communicate via the Internet Gateway.
items.exp: Data transferred between EC2/ECS instances within the same Availability Zone using private IP addresses is $0.00/GB, whereas cross-AZ data transfer costs $0.01/GB in each direction ($0.02/GB total). By enabling AZ-aware routing (Kafka rack awareness `client.rack` mapped to the physical `az-id` like `use1-az1`, or service-mesh/load-balancer AZ affinity), consumers read from local same-AZ replicas at zero data-transfer cost while retaining full Multi-AZ failover.

items.q: Mammoth Capital distributes daily financial research videos and interactive chart bundles (stored in an Amazon S3 bucket in `us-east-1` and dynamically rendered by EC2 instances) to 250,000 global subscribers across North America, Europe, and Asia. Currently, subscribers download directly from the S3 bucket and EC2 Application Load Balancer in `us-east-1`, generating 150 TB/month of Internet Data Transfer Out (DTO) and causing regional edge caches in Europe and Asia to repeatedly hit the `us-east-1` EC2 origin simultaneously whenever a report drops. What architecture change reduces both the Data Transfer Out cost and the duplicate cache-fill load on the `us-east-1` origin?
opts: Deploy AWS Global Accelerator in front of the S3 bucket.
Place an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket (using Origin Access Control) and the ALB origin, and enable CloudFront Origin Shield in `us-east-1`.
Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication to 12 AWS Regions and have clients query all 12 buckets round-robin.
Replace the Application Load Balancer with an AWS Direct Connect connection to a local ISP.
items.exp: Amazon CloudFront caches content at 600+ global edge POPs, charges nothing ($0.00/GB) for origin data transfer from S3/ALB into CloudFront, offers lower tiered DTO rates (and Price Classes / Security Savings Bundle discounts), and CloudFront Origin Shield adds a centralized caching layer in `us-east-1` that collapses concurrent cache misses from global Regional Edge Caches into a single origin request.

items.q: Mammoth Capital runs 40 self-managed TimescaleDB nodes on Amazon EC2. Each node needs only 400 GB of actual disk storage, but because the database requires a sustained baseline of 9,000 IOPS and 250 MB/s of throughput, the previous engineer provisioned a 3,000 GB (3 TB) General Purpose SSD (`gp2`) EBS volume on every instance solely to scale the `gp2` baseline performance (at 3 IOPS/GB). As a result, 86% of the provisioned disk space sits empty while costing $12,000/month across the fleet. How can the architect cut this EBS storage bill by more than 65% without losing any IOPS or throughput?
opts: Create right-sized 500 GB `gp3` volumes provisioned with 9,000 IOPS and 250 MB/s (gp3 includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s at a 20% lower per-GB price), copy each node's data onto them, and delete the 3 TB `gp2` volumes (EBS volumes cannot shrink in place).
Convert the volumes from `gp2` to Cold HDD (`sc1`) using EBS Elastic Volumes.
Migrate the TimescaleDB data directories onto Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval using an NFS gateway.
Convert the volumes from `gp2` to Provisioned IOPS SSD (`io2` Block Express) kept at 3,000 GB per node.
items.exp: Unlike `gp2` (which ties baseline IOPS to volume size at 3 IOPS/GB and caps throughput at 250 MB/s), `gp3` costs 20% less per GB, includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s regardless of size, and lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently. A 500 GB `gp3` volume with 9,000 IOPS and 250 MB/s costs roughly a quarter of a 3 TB `gp2` volume. Elastic Volumes can change a volume's type in place but cannot make it smaller, so right-sizing means new volumes plus a data copy.

items.q: To satisfy a regulatory record-keeping rule, Mammoth Capital must take a monthly point-in-time EBS snapshot of 120 production database volumes (totaling 100 TB of full block data) and retain each monthly snapshot for 7 years. In practice, these historical monthly snapshots are almost never restored unless an auditor requests a forensic look-back older than 6 months. However, keeping 84 monthly snapshots in the standard EBS Snapshot tier is costing thousands of dollars per month because blocks slowly churn over the years. What native AWS feature can reduce the storage cost of these long-term, rarely restored EBS snapshots by up to 75%?
opts: Configure Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) to automatically create the monthly snapshots and transition them to the Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive tier (which offers up to 75% lower storage cost for full snapshots retained ≥90 days).
Enable Amazon EBS Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR) on all 84 monthly snapshots across three Availability Zones.
Copy the EBS snapshots across three AWS Regions every month using AWS Backup.
Attach 84 extra `gp2` EBS volumes to a stopped EC2 instance and `dd` the raw blocks onto them.
items.exp: Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive is a low-cost storage tier ($0.0125/GB-month vs $0.05/GB-month—up to 75% cheaper) for full, point-in-time EBS snapshots that must be retained for 90 days or longer for compliance and are rarely restored (taking 24–72 hours to restore back to the standard tier). Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) can automate both creation and archival.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's core trade-confirmation ledger runs on an Amazon DynamoDB table (`trade-confirmations`). Over the past 18 months, traffic has been rock-steady 24/7 at 25,000 Write Capacity Units (WCUs) and 50,000 Read Capacity Units (RCUs) with gentle, predictable 15% diurnal rises during market open. When the table was first created as a prototype, the developer selected DynamoDB On-Demand capacity mode and never changed it. How should the architect optimize the monthly DynamoDB throughput bill for the next 12 months?
opts: Switch the table to Provisioned Capacity mode with DynamoDB Auto Scaling (target utilization 70%) and purchase 1-year DynamoDB Reserved Capacity for the baseline WCUs and RCUs.
Keep the table in On-Demand capacity mode and purchase EC2 Compute Savings Plans.
Deploy Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached in front of the table to buffer all 25,000 writes per second before writing to DynamoDB once a week.
Enable DynamoDB Global Tables across four AWS Regions to divide the write load by four.
items.exp: DynamoDB On-Demand is ideal for spiky, unpredictable, or low-volume workloads, but for steady, predictable high-throughput workloads, switching to Provisioned Capacity mode with Auto Scaling and purchasing 1-year or 3-year DynamoDB Reserved Capacity reduces throughput costs by 53% to 77% compared to On-Demand.

items.q: Mammoth Capital has 15 non-production Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL clusters used by QA engineers only on weekdays between 08:00 and 18:00 local time (50 hours/week out of 168 hours/week) and intermittent internal hackathon tools that go days with zero queries, yet must spin back up automatically within a few seconds when a developer runs a test without losing connection strings. Previously, the team tried manually stopping RDS instances on Friday evenings, but AWS automatically restarts stopped RDS instances after 7 days during long holidays, and developers often forgot to stop them at night. What is the lowest-maintenance way to minimize compute costs for these spiky and frequently idle Aurora clusters?
opts: Purchase 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instances (`db.r6g.4xlarge`) for all 15 non-production QA clusters.

Migrate the non-production clusters to Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 and configure `MinCapacity = 0` ACUs (auto-pause after an idle timeout) so compute scales to zero ($0.00/hour for ACUs) whenever idle and resumes automatically on the next database connection.
Take a manual final snapshot every night at 18:00, delete all 15 Aurora clusters, and restore them from snapshots every morning at 07:00 using Jenkins.
Convert the Aurora PostgreSQL clusters into Multi-AZ DB Clusters with two readable standbys.
items.exp: Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 supports scaling down to `0` ACUs (auto-pause) after a configurable period of inactivity. When paused (`0` ACUs), you pay only for Aurora storage and zero compute charges, and when a new database connection arrives, the cluster automatically resumes and scales ACUs in sub-second increments.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's primary settlement database runs on an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster (`db.r6g.8xlarge` writer and two `db.r6g.8xlarge` readers) using the `Aurora Standard` storage configuration. Because the settlement engine performs intense write-ahead logging and random index lookups across a 12 TB dataset, monthly `Aurora:StorageIOUsage` charges ($0.20 per 1 million I/O requests) have surged to $28,000/month out of a $62,000/month total Aurora bill (45% of the cluster's spend). What single configuration change can the DBA make with zero application code changes to lower the total monthly Aurora bill and achieve predictable pricing?
opts: Switch the cluster storage configuration from `Aurora Standard` to `Aurora I/O-Optimized`, which eliminates all per-request read/write I/O charges and saves money whenever I/O spend exceeds 25% of total Aurora database spend.
Add four more `db.r6g.8xlarge` Aurora Replicas in the same Availability Zone.
Enable Aurora Backtrack with a 72-hour target window.
Disable the PostgreSQL query planner and force full-table sequential scans on every query.
items.exp: Amazon Aurora I/O-Optimized charges $0.00 for read and write I/O operations in exchange for a modestly higher compute (~30%) and storage rate. As a rule of thumb, whenever I/O charges exceed 25% of your total Aurora database spend (here it is 45%), switching the cluster to `Aurora I/O-Optimized` delivers immediate net savings (up to 40%) and predictable monthly bills.

items.q: Last month, a developer in Mammoth Capital's Quantitative Sandbox account accidentally left a recursive AWS Step Functions Express workflow running over a weekend, burning $19,000 in 48 hours before anyone looked at Cost Explorer on Monday morning. Because Mammoth's overall AWS Organization spend fluctuates naturally between $12,000/day and $18,000/day depending on market volatility, a simple static threshold alarm on total account spend either triggers false alarms on busy trading days or misses a $400/hour spike in an unusual service like Step Functions or Textract. Which native AWS FinOps service uses machine learning on historical spend patterns to automatically detect anomalous spend spikes by individual AWS service, member account, or cost allocation tag and alert a Slack channel via Amazon SNS?
opts: AWS Price List Bulk API
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
AWS Trusted Advisor Service Quotas check
AWS Artifact
items.exp: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses multi-layered machine learning models trained on your historical spend trends (accounting for weekly/seasonal periodicity) to evaluate spend across AWS services, member accounts, Cost Categories, or Cost Allocation Tags multiple times per day, sending root-cause alerts via Amazon SNS or email when an anomalous dollar or percentage spike occurs.

items.q: Mammoth Capital gives each of its 25 quantitative interns a dedicated AWS sandbox member account inside an `Intern-Sandboxes` Organizational Unit (OU) with a strict monthly allowance of $300 per account. Previously, they configured a standard AWS Budget notification email at 80% and 100% of $300, but an intern ignored the Saturday night email after launching a `p4d.24xlarge` GPU instance ($32.77/hour), racking up $1,800 before Monday morning. How can the platform team configure AWS Budgets so that the moment an intern account's actual cost hits 100% of $300, AWS automatically stops existing EC2/RDS instances and blocks the intern from launching any new EC2, RDS, or SageMaker resources until an administrator resets it?
opts: Configure AWS Cost Explorer Rightsizing Recommendations to email the CFO at the end of the billing month.
Enable AWS Compute Optimizer with an S3 Bucket Policy.

Configure an AWS Budget Action on the $300 monthly budget that automatically applies an IAM policy or AWS Organizations Service Control Policy (SCP) denying resource creation and/or executes an SSM action to stop target EC2/RDS instances when the 100% actual threshold is breached.
Purchase a 1-year Compute Savings Plan for $300/month.
items.exp: AWS Budgets supports automated **Budget Actions**: when a budget threshold (actual or forecasted) is breached, Budgets can automatically attach a restrictive IAM policy to a user/role/group, apply a Service Control Policy (SCP) to an account/OU (blocking new EC2/RDS/SageMaker launches), or stop specific EC2 or RDS instances—either automatically or with approval.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's Finance Committee wants an automated, executive-ready BI dashboard that breaks down AWS cloud costs down to the hourly line-item level by custom business unit tags (`CostCenter`, `StrategyDesk`, `Environment`), includes amortized Reserved Instance and Savings Plan effective rates (`SavingsPlanEffectiveCost`), and joins those hourly resource costs with Mammoth's internal per-desk trading revenue CSV stored in Amazon S3. Which AWS architecture is the standard, most cost-effective solution for building this granular FinOps reporting pipeline?
opts: Manually export CSVs from the AWS Billing Console every Friday and email them to the Finance Committee.
Stream VPC Flow Logs into Amazon OpenSearch Service (`r6g.12xlarge` cluster) and estimate EC2 costs from packet counts.
Query the AWS CloudTrail `LookupEvents` API every 5 minutes from a Lambda function and multiply API calls by list prices.

Activate user-defined Cost Allocation Tags, configure AWS Data Exports (Cost and Usage Report / CUR 2.0) to deliver Parquet-formatted hourly line items with resource IDs into an Amazon S3 bucket, catalog the data with AWS Glue/Athena, and visualize the joined cost-and-revenue datasets in Amazon QuickSight.
items.exp: The AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR / Data Exports CUR 2.0) is the most granular source of AWS billing data, capturing hourly/daily line-item usage, resource IDs, user-defined Cost Allocation Tags, and amortized Savings Plan/RI rates in Apache Parquet format in Amazon S3. Querying CUR in place with Amazon Athena and visualizing it in Amazon QuickSight (such as the Cloud Intelligence Dashboards / CUDOS) is the AWS-recommended FinOps pattern.

items.q: A solo engineer runs a web-scraping and threat-intelligence cluster of 30 dual-stack (IPv4 + IPv6) Ubuntu EC2 instances in private subnets. The instances download 80 TB/month of public archive feeds from external servers that fully support IPv6 (`AAAA` DNS records). Currently, all outbound traffic from the private subnets routes through a Managed NAT Gateway, costing $3,600/month in NAT Gateway data processing charges ($0.045/GB for 80 TB). The private EC2 instances must remain unreachable from inbound connections initiated on the internet. How can the engineer eliminate the $3,600/month NAT Gateway data processing charge for all IPv6-capable external destinations?
opts: Attach an Egress-Only Internet Gateway to the VPC, assign IPv6 global unicast addresses from the VPC's `/56` IPv6 CIDR block to the private subnets, and add a `::/0` route pointing to the Egress-Only Internet Gateway (which has $0.00/hour and $0.00/GB data processing fees).
Replace the Managed NAT Gateway with an AWS Transit Gateway connected to a Site-to-Site VPN.
Assign public IPv4 Elastic IPs to all 30 instances and open `0.0.0.0/0` on all inbound ports in the Security Group.
Create an S3 VPC Gateway Endpoint and route external internet scraping traffic through it.
items.exp: An Egress-Only Internet Gateway is a stateful, horizontally scaled VPC component exclusively for IPv6 traffic: it allows instances in private subnets to initiate outbound IPv6 connections to the internet while blocking all unsolicited inbound IPv6 connections from the internet, and AWS charges $0.00/hour and $0.00/GB for Egress-Only Internet Gateway data processing.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's compliance analysts run 2,500 ad-hoc SQL queries per day using Amazon Athena against a 50 TB table of uncompressed, unpartitioned CSV trade logs stored in Amazon S3. Most queries filter on a single trading date (`WHERE trade_date = '2026-10-15'`) and select only 4 out of 60 columns (`symbol`, `price`, `qty`, `venue`). Because Athena charges $5.00 per TB of data scanned, every single query scans all 50 TB of uncompressed CSVs ($250 per query!), threatening to blow the analytics budget. How can the data engineering team reduce Athena's per-query data scanned (and cost) by more than 98% while also making queries run 10x faster?
opts: Move the uncompressed CSV files from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Deep Archive and query them directly with Athena.

Use an AWS Glue ETL job (or Athena `CTAS`) to convert the raw CSVs into compressed columnar Apache Parquet (or ORC) format with Snappy/Zstandard compression and partition the S3 prefixes by `trade_date` (`s3://.../trade_date=YYYY-MM-DD/`).
Concatenate all 50 TB of CSV files into a single 50 TB uncompressed `.txt` file and disable S3 Versioning.
Provision an Amazon Redshift cluster with sixteen `ra3.16xlarge` nodes to run 24/7.
items.exp: Amazon Athena bills $5.00 per TB of data scanned. Partitioning by `trade_date` lets Athena skip scanning 99%+ of dates (partition pruning), while converting from row-oriented uncompressed CSV to a compressed columnar format (Apache Parquet or ORC) shrinks file size by 70–85% and lets Athena read only the 4 requested columns out of 60—commonly reducing scanned bytes and cost by 98–99.9%.

items.q: Mammoth Capital has an Amazon SQS queue that receives 80 million order-lifecycle JSON events per day from an exchange gateway. An AWS Lambda function (`x86_64`, 1,024 MB) polls the SQS queue via an Event Source Mapping, parses each JSON message, and immediately exits (`return`) on 92% of messages because the function only needs to process events where `"eventType": "TRADE_REJECTED"` and `"notionalUsd" > 50000`. As a result, 92% of Mammoth's Lambda request and duration charges are wasted on no-op invocations. What two configuration changes can eliminate the wasted invocations and lower the cost of the remaining 8% of executions?
opts: Increase the Lambda function memory to 10,240 MB and set the SQS visibility timeout to 0 seconds.
Replace the SQS queue with an Amazon RDS for Oracle instance and poll it every millisecond from Lambda.

Configure Lambda Event Source Mapping event filtering (`FilterCriteria`) on the SQS trigger to match only `eventType = TRADE_REJECTED` and `notionalUsd > 50000` (which filters messages for free before invoking Lambda), and switch the Lambda runtime architecture to `arm64` (AWS Graviton2).
Enable Provisioned Concurrency of 1,000 concurrent executions 24/7 on the Lambda function.
items.exp: Lambda Event Source Mapping `FilterCriteria` evaluates JSON pattern rules (including string matching and numeric comparisons) against SQS, Kinesis, and DynamoDB Streams payloads at zero additional charge before invoking your function—eliminating 92% of invocations—while switching Lambda to `arm64` (Graviton2) reduces GB-second duration price by 20% and improves price-performance up to 34%.

items.q: A quantitative researcher maintains a self-hosted Proxmox VE homelab with a 40 TB ZFS NAS connected to their VPC via an existing 1 Gbps site-to-site fiber link with 600 Mbps of idle capacity overnight (22:00 to 06:00). Every night, their local GPU rig generates 1.5 TB of new compressed model checkpoints across 200,000 files while modifying 5% of existing files. Previously, a bash script ran `aws s3 cp --recursive` every night, which wasted bandwidth and S3 `PUT` request fees re-uploading unchanged files and choked on single-threaded metadata listings. What is the most cost-effective managed AWS service to transfer only incremental changed files overnight over the existing link into Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval while throttling bandwidth during daytime hours?
opts: Order a new AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device every afternoon for overnight courier delivery.
Enable Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration and continue re-uploading all 40 TB every night with `aws s3 cp --recursive`.
Provision an AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway (VTL) and write virtual magnetic tapes to S3 Standard.

Deploy the AWS DataSync agent as a VM on the local Proxmox VE cluster, configure a scheduled nightly DataSync task with built-in bandwidth throttling to transfer only incremental changes directly into S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.
items.exp: AWS DataSync deploys as a light VM agent (supporting KVM/Proxmox, VMware, Hyper-V) and uses a parallelized, purpose-built transfer protocol to copy only incremental file changes (`TransferMode=CHANGED`), validate checksums inline, enforce time-of-day bandwidth throttling, and write directly into any S3 storage class (including S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval) without extra S3 lifecycle transition fees.

items.q: Mammoth Capital is moving its algorithmic trading platform to AWS. Which characteristic of cloud computing best addresses their need for massive compute bursts during market open?
opts: High Availability
Elasticity
Agility
Global Reach
items.exp: Elasticity allows Mammoth to dynamically scale resources in and out to meet sudden spikes in demand, like the market open. High Availability is about uptime, Agility is speed to market, Global Reach is geography.

opts: OpEx to CapEx
CapEx to OpEx
Fixed to Variable
CapEx to Variable
items.exp: Cloud computing shifts Capital Expenses (CapEx) to Variable Expenses, allowing them to pay only for what they consume, unlike physical servers which require large upfront CapEx.

items.q: Which AWS pricing model allows Mammoth Capital to bid on spare EC2 capacity to run stateless backtesting algorithms cheaply?
opts: On-Demand
Reserved Instances
Spot Instances
Dedicated Hosts
items.exp: Spot Instances provide up to 90% discount for fault-tolerant, stateless workloads like backtesting. On-Demand is for unpredictable steady workloads, Reserved is for 1-3 year commitments.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's European subsidiary collects personal data from clients in Germany, and GDPR compliance strictly forbids that data from leaving the European Union. Meanwhile, their US trading desk stores data in us-east-1 (Northern Virginia). Which statement accurately describes how AWS Regions handle this requirement?
opts: Each AWS Region is completely independent, so data stored in eu-central-1 (Frankfurt) stays in that Region unless you explicitly replicate it elsewhere.
AWS automatically replicates all S3 and database data across every global Region by default for durability.
Regions within the same hemisphere share a single unified data center and power grid, while cross-hemisphere Regions replicate asynchronously.
Data residency is enforced at the Availability Zone level rather than the Region level because AZs span multiple countries.
items.exp: AWS Regions are completely independent geographic areas, and data stored in one Region never automatically replicates to another. Selecting eu-central-1 ensures EU client data stays within the EU for GDPR compliance.

items.q: A solutions architect at Mammoth Capital deploys a critical order-matching API onto a single EC2 instance in one Availability Zone (us-east-1a). During a severe storm, a power substation feeding that data center fails. What happens to the API, and how should the architecture be fixed?
opts: The API stays online because a single Availability Zone automatically spans multiple independent power grids across different cities.
AWS automatically live-migrates the running EC2 instance to eu-central-1 over the public internet with zero downtime.
The API goes offline because a single AZ is a single point of failure; production workloads must span at least two AZs in the same Region.
The API remains available as long as the instance is vertically scaled to a larger size within the same Availability Zone.
items.exp: Each Availability Zone is a physically separate data center with its own power and flood plain, making a single-AZ deployment a single point of failure. Deploying across at least two AZs in the same Region keeps the workload running over low-latency fiber if one AZ goes dark.

items.q: When designing a new low-latency trading portal for clients in Singapore, Mammoth Capital's architect must choose an AWS Region first. According to AWS architecture principles, what are the two primary factors that govern which Region to select?
opts: The number of hypervisor slices per server and the age of the physical cooling equipment.
Whether the workload runs on bare metal servers or Docker containers.
The automatic cross-region replication speed and the local electricity utility rate.
Proximity to end users (latency) and legal or regulatory data residency requirements (compliance).
items.exp: You choose an AWS Region based on latency (placing infrastructure close to your users) and compliance (satisfying legal mandates like GDPR that dictate where data physically lives).

items.q: Before moving to AWS, Mammoth Capital spent $2,000,000 upfront on physical servers, storage arrays, and switches that sat on the balance sheet as depreciating assets for five years. In financial terms, how does migrating these workloads to pay-by-the-second cloud infrastructure shift their IT spending?
opts: From variable operational expenditure (OpEx) to fixed capital expenditure (CapEx).
From upfront capital expenditure (CapEx) to variable operational expenditure (OpEx) that scales with consumption.
From depreciating operational expenses to non-depreciating hardware assets.
From per-second variable billing to a mandatory 5-year fixed hardware lease.
items.exp: Buying physical data center hardware is Capital Expenditure (CapEx) requiring massive upfront outlay and multi-year depreciation. The cloud shifts this to Operational Expenditure (OpEx), where you pay by the second for what you use with zero upfront hardware cost.
items.topic: The Financial Shift: CapEx vs OpEx

items.q: Mammoth Capital's CFO is skeptical about migrating a compute cluster to AWS, arguing that buying physical servers for the office server room looks cheaper on a 5-year spreadsheet if run at 100% capacity. Based on the CapEx vs. OpEx model, what is the strongest financial argument for the cloud?
opts: Cloud servers are always cheaper per core than physical hardware even at 100% utilization 24/7 for five years.
AWS allows the company to capitalize monthly EC2 bills as physical hardware assets on the balance sheet.
CapEx eliminates the need to estimate capacity in advance, whereas OpEx requires guessing capacity three years ahead.
Traditional CapEx forces you to guess peak capacity years in advance and pay for idle hardware, whereas OpEx lets you stop paying the second you shut down unused resources.
items.exp: Cloud is not always cheaper on raw unit cost, but it is elastic. Instead of over-provisioning fixed CapEx hardware years in advance, you trade a fixed, over-provisioned cost for a variable OpEx cost that scales with revenue and drops to zero when resources are shut down.
items.topic: The Financial Shift: CapEx vs OpEx

items.q: In a traditional CapEx IT model, an engineering team must guess its hardware capacity needs three years in advance. What are the two classic failure modes of this upfront capacity guess?
opts: Guessing too low causes the system to crash during peak events, while guessing too high leaves the company paying for idle servers for years.
Guessing too low increases monthly depreciation taxes, while guessing too high triggers automatic AWS bandwidth throttling.
Guessing too low converts CapEx into OpEx automatically, while guessing too high voids hardware warranties.
Guessing too low forces workloads into containers, while guessing too high prevents vertical scaling.
items.exp: When you buy hardware upfront, under-estimating capacity crashes your site during your biggest sales or trading events, while over-estimating leaves you paying for idle servers for years.
items.topic: The Financial Shift: CapEx vs OpEx

items.q: Mammoth Capital's interns need access to an S3 bucket to analyze historical tick data. Which IAM entity should you attach the policy to?
opts: IAM User
IAM Role
IAM Group
Root User
items.exp: Policies for multiple users with the same needs (like interns) should be attached to an IAM Group for easier management. Roles are assumed, not given directly to interns unless via SSO.

items.q: An application running on an EC2 instance needs to read secrets from AWS Secrets Manager. What is the most secure way to grant this permission?
opts: Store access keys in the EC2 instance metadata
Attach an IAM Role to the EC2 instance
Hardcode an IAM User's access keys in the app code
Create an inline policy for the EC2 instance
items.exp: IAM Roles are the most secure way to grant permissions to EC2 instances. Access keys should never be stored in metadata or code.

items.q: Which IAM feature adds an extra layer of security on top of a username and password, highly recommended for the root account of Mammoth Capital?
opts: MFA
Access Keys
Password Policy
IAM Access Analyzer
items.exp: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) requires a second form of verification, critical for securing high-privilege accounts like root.

items.q: Mammoth Capital runs a web portal where requests to https://portal.mammoth.com/api must be routed to a fleet of trading API instances, while requests to https://portal.mammoth.com/static must go to a separate group of media servers. Which load balancer should the architect choose?
opts: Network Load Balancer (NLB) operating at Layer 4.
Gateway Load Balancer (GLB) inspecting raw packets.
Application Load Balancer (ALB) operating at Layer 7 with path-based routing.
A round-robin list of six public IP addresses handed directly to clients.
items.exp: Application Load Balancer (ALB) operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) and inspects application content to route traffic based on URL paths (such as /api vs /static), host headers, query strings, or cookies.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's high-frequency order ingestion engine communicates over a custom TCP/UDP protocol rather than HTTP, requires static IP addresses, and must handle millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency. Which AWS load balancer is built for this?
opts: Network Load Balancer (NLB)
Application Load Balancer (ALB)
Gateway Load Balancer (GLB)
Bastion Host Jump Box
items.exp: Network Load Balancer (NLB) operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) with no HTTP content inspection, forwarding raw traffic at millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency.

items.q: Six EC2 instances sit behind a Load Balancer serving Mammoth Capital's client dashboard. At 2:15 PM, Instance #4 suffers an OS freeze and stops responding. How does the Load Balancer keep users from hitting that dead server?
opts: It SSHes into Instance #4 and restarts the web daemon automatically.
It runs periodic Health Checks every few seconds and immediately removes any non-responsive server from rotation.
It caches the entire backend database in Layer 4 memory so EC2 instances are no longer needed.
It routes failed requests through a Gateway Load Balancer third-party IDS appliance to reconstruct the HTTP response.
items.exp: Every few seconds, the Load Balancer pings each backend server with a health check. If an instance stops responding, the Load Balancer immediately removes it from rotation so user traffic never hits the dead server.

items.q: Mammoth Capital configures an Auto Scaling Group for its web tier so that it never runs fewer than 2 instances at 3 AM on a Tuesday, and never spins up more than 20 instances during a market panic so the budget stays protected. Which two ASG settings enforce these boundaries?
opts: Health Check Grace Period and Cooldown Timer
Target Group Weight and Sticky Session Duration
AMI Bootstrap Script and CloudWatch Log Retention
Minimum capacity (2) and Maximum capacity (20)
items.exp: Minimum capacity defines the floor (never run fewer than 2 instances), while Maximum capacity sets the ceiling (never exceed 20 instances) to protect your budget.

items.q: During a sudden market rally, average CPU across Mammoth Capital's EC2 fleet exceeds 70% for 3 consecutive minutes. What happens when the Auto Scaling Group's scaling policy is triggered?
opts: The ASG pauses incoming traffic at the Internet Gateway until existing instances cool down below 70% CPU.
The ASG acts on the CloudWatch metric, launches new instances from your AMI, registers them with the Load Balancer, and scales back in when the spike passes.
The ASG upgrades the CPU and RAM of the running EC2 instances in place without launching new instances.
The ASG emails the on-call engineer a list of AMIs so they can manually launch and attach instances to the Load Balancer.
items.exp: The ASG monitors CloudWatch metrics and automatically launches new instances bootstrapped with your AMI, registers them with the Load Balancer to absorb traffic, and terminates the extra instances to stop billing once load drops.

items.q: An architect wants to deploy a web application that distributes incoming requests across servers, automatically scales compute capacity out and in with demand, and survives an Availability Zone outage. What is the canonical AWS architecture triad for this?
opts: Single-AZ EC2 + Vertical Scaling + NAT Gateway
Gateway Load Balancer + Dedicated Host + Manual AMI Snapshots
Application Load Balancer (ALB) + Auto Scaling Group (ASG) + Multi-AZ EC2 fleet
Route 53 Simple Routing + Single large EC2 instance + Elastic IP
items.exp: The triad of an Application Load Balancer (traffic distribution), an Auto Scaling Group (elastic capacity), and a Multi-AZ EC2 fleet (fault tolerance across data centers) is the standard architecture for resilient, cost-efficient web apps.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's institutional clients connect to an order-entry API over HTTPS. Several clients operate legacy enterprise firewalls that can only whitelist fixed IPv4 addresses, yet Mammoth's backend relies on URL path-based routing (/equities vs /options) across different ECS services. Which architecture meets both requirements?
opts: Assign Elastic IPs directly to the Application Load Balancer nodes in each Availability Zone
Place a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IPs in front of an Application Load Balancer configured as its target
Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Gateway Load Balancer using GENEVE encapsulation
Use a Network Load Balancer alone and configure path-based routing rules on its TCP listener
items.exp: ALBs do not support static or Elastic IPs, and NLBs cannot inspect Layer 7 URL paths. Putting an NLB (with Elastic IPs per AZ) in front of an ALB gives clients fixed IPs to whitelist while preserving ALB path-based routing.
items.topic: Load Balancer Family: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB

items.q: A security architect wants to inspect all ingress and egress traffic across multiple VPCs using a scalable fleet of third-party intrusion detection virtual appliances without changing client IP addresses. Which load balancer is purpose-built for this?
opts: Application Load Balancer (ALB) with AWS WAF attached
Network Load Balancer (NLB) with TLS passthrough enabled
Classic Load Balancer (CLB) in TCP proxy mode
Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) encapsulating traffic with the GENEVE protocol
items.exp: GWLB deploys, scales, and manages third-party virtual appliances inline. It encapsulates original Layer 3 packets inside GENEVE (UDP port 6081) so appliances can inspect traffic transparently.
items.topic: Load Balancer Family: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB

items.q: An engineering team deploys a Network Load Balancer across two Availability Zones. AZ-A has 1 EC2 instance and AZ-B has 9 EC2 instances, with Cross-Zone Load Balancing left at its default setting. How will incoming traffic be distributed if Route 53 sends 50% of requests to each AZ?
opts: Each of the 10 instances receives 10% of the traffic automatically, with no extra data transfer charge
Each of the 10 instances receives 10% of the traffic, but inter-AZ data transfer charges apply
The single instance in AZ-A receives 50% of the traffic, while the 9 instances in AZ-B split the remaining 50%
The NLB automatically migrates 4 instances from AZ-B to AZ-A to balance the fleet
items.exp: On NLB, Cross-Zone Load Balancing is disabled by default. Each NLB node only distributes traffic to targets within its own AZ, so the lone instance in AZ-A absorbs the entire 50% hitting AZ-A.
items.topic: Load Balancer Family: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB

items.q: Mammoth Capital's trading engine is in a private subnet. It needs to download OS updates from the internet but must not allow incoming connections. What should you use?
opts: Internet Gateway
NAT Gateway
Egress-Only Internet Gateway
VPC Peering
items.exp: A NAT Gateway allows instances in a private subnet to connect to the internet (for updates) but prevents the internet from initiating connections. Egress-Only is for IPv6.

items.q: To protect their database tier, Mammoth Capital wants to block traffic from a specific known malicious IP address. Which VPC component is designed for this?
opts: Security Group
Network ACL
Route Table
NAT Gateway
items.exp: Network ACLs (NACLs) are stateless and support explicit DENY rules, perfect for blocking specific IPs. Security Groups are stateful and only support ALLOW rules.

items.q: Which of these acts like a virtual firewall at the instance level, similar to a pfSense firewall but for individual EC2 instances?
opts: Network ACL
Security Group
WAF
Shield
items.exp: Security Groups act as virtual firewalls at the instance (ENI) level. NACLs act at the subnet level. WAF is for web exploits.

items.q: A junior engineer at Mammoth Capital launches an EC2 instance inside a public subnet whose Route Table has a 0.0.0.0/0 route pointing to the VPC's Internet Gateway, yet the instance still cannot connect to the internet. Security groups and NACLs allow the traffic. What is missing?
opts: The EC2 instance is missing a public IP address (Elastic IP or auto-assigned public IP); both an IGW route and a public IP are required.
The subnet also requires a NAT Gateway attached directly to the instance's private network interface.
Public subnets cannot communicate outbound unless traffic passes through a Bastion Host first.
The Internet Gateway must be placed inside a private subnet before it can route traffic.
items.exp: To reach the internet from a public subnet, an EC2 instance requires both a Route Table entry pointing to the Internet Gateway and a public IP address (auto-assigned or Elastic IP); missing either one breaks connectivity.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's PostgreSQL database and application servers sit in a private subnet with no route to the Internet Gateway. The application servers need to download OS updates and call an external market-data API over the internet while remaining completely unreachable from inbound internet traffic. How should this be architected?
opts: Deploy a NAT Gateway in the private subnet and point the public subnet's Route Table to it.
Attach an Internet Gateway route directly to the private subnet's Route Table and assign public IPs to the database.
Deploy a Bastion Host in the private subnet to proxy all outbound database traffic.
Deploy a NAT Gateway in the public subnet and route outbound traffic from the private subnet through it.
items.exp: A NAT Gateway deployed in the public subnet acts as a one-way valve, allowing instances in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet for updates and API calls without ever being reachable inbound.

items.q: What single configuration difference determines whether a VPC subnet is a Public Subnet or a Private Subnet, and how should an engineer securely SSH into an EC2 instance in that Private Subnet?
opts: Whether the instances run Linux or Windows; SSH directly to the database's public IP.
Whether the subnet's Route Table has a route (0.0.0.0/0) to an Internet Gateway; SSH first to a hardened Bastion Host (Jump Box) in the public subnet and hop from there.
Whether the subnet is in us-east-1a or us-east-1b; SSH through the NAT Gateway's inbound port.
Whether Security Groups are enabled; assign an temporary public IP to the private subnet Route Table.
items.exp: A subnet is public only if its Route Table has a route to an Internet Gateway; private subnets have no IGW route, so the sanctioned SSH entry point is a hardened Bastion Host (Jump Box) in the public subnet.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's EC2 instances in a locked-down private subnet upload and download terabytes of historical tick files to Amazon S3 every day. Their compliance auditor forbids this traffic from touching the public internet, and the CFO wants to eliminate the NAT Gateway per-GB charges. What should the architect configure?
opts: Add an Internet Gateway to the private subnet and assign Elastic IPs to the EC2 instances.
Deploy a second NAT Gateway in another Availability Zone to split the bandwidth bill.
Create a VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3 and add a route to it in the private subnet's Route Table at zero cost.
Set up a Bastion Host in the public subnet and tunnel all S3 uploads over SSH.
items.exp: A VPC Gateway Endpoint routes S3 or DynamoDB traffic privately over Amazon's backbone network via a Route Table entry, bypassing both the public internet and NAT Gateway data charges completely for free.

items.q: An application running in an isolated private subnet with no NAT Gateway needs to retrieve secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and send messages to Amazon SQS over AWS's private network. Which VPC Endpoint type is required, and how does it work?
opts: An Interface Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink), which creates an Elastic Network Interface (ENI) with a private IP inside your subnet for a small hourly per-AZ charge.
A Gateway Endpoint, which is free and supports all AWS services through a Route Table entry.
A NAT Gateway Endpoint, which translates private IPs into public S3 bucket policies.
An Internet Gateway Endpoint, which assigns a public IP directly to Secrets Manager.
items.exp: Gateway Endpoints only work with S3 and DynamoDB. Almost every other AWS service—including Secrets Manager, SQS, SNS, and KMS—uses an Interface Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink), which provisions an ENI with a private IP in your subnet.

items.q: You are comparing VPC Gateway Endpoints and VPC Interface Endpoints during an architecture review. Which statement accurately contrasts the two?
opts: Gateway Endpoints create an ENI in your subnet and charge per hour, whereas Interface Endpoints modify Route Tables and are free.
Gateway Endpoints work only with SQS and SNS, whereas Interface Endpoints work only with S3 and DynamoDB.
Gateway Endpoints route traffic over the public internet via NAT, whereas Interface Endpoints stay on the AWS backbone.
Gateway Endpoints are free, Route-Table-based, and work only with S3 and DynamoDB, whereas Interface Endpoints use a private-IP ENI, charge per hour/AZ, and support most other AWS services.
items.exp: Gateway Endpoints are free, configured in your Route Table, and support only S3 and DynamoDB, whereas Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink) place a private-IP ENI in your subnet, carry an hourly per-AZ fee, and support dozens of other AWS services.

items.q: Mammoth Capital needs an EC2 instance to run a high-performance database with massive IOPS requirements for their order matching engine. Which instance family is best?
opts: T3 (Burstable)
R5 (Memory-Optimized)
I3 (Storage-Optimized)
C5 (Compute-Optimized)
items.exp: Storage-Optimized (I series) instances provide high, sequential read and write access to very large data sets on local storage, ideal for high IOPS databases. R is for in-memory, C is for compute.

items.q: For a predictable, steady-state workload running their risk management dashboard 24/7 for the next 3 years, which pricing model is most cost-effective?
opts: On-Demand
Spot
Dedicated Hosts
Reserved Instances
items.exp: Reserved Instances (RIs) offer the highest discount for predictable, long-term (1-3 year) commitments. Spot is too risky for steady state, On-Demand is too expensive.

items.q: What EC2 feature allows you to place instances on a dedicated physical server to meet strict financial compliance requirements?
opts: Dedicated Instances
Dedicated Hosts
Placement Groups
Bare Metal
items.exp: Dedicated Hosts provide visibility and control over how instances are placed on physical servers, essential for strict compliance and BYOL licensing. Dedicated Instances just run on single-tenant hardware.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's quantitative research team wants to run a monolithic backtesting job that takes 2 hours to execute and requires 32 GB of RAM in a single execution environment. Why is AWS Lambda the wrong compute choice for this workload?
opts: Lambda can only be triggered by S3 uploads and cannot execute Python or Java code.
Lambda has a hard maximum execution time of 15 minutes and a maximum memory limit of 10 GB.
Lambda charges a flat 24/7 hourly rate even when no functions are executing.
Lambda is permanently capped at 10 concurrent executions per AWS account.
items.exp: AWS Lambda enforces hard limits of 15 minutes maximum execution time and 10 GB maximum memory per function, making a 2-hour, 32 GB workload impossible to run in a single Lambda invocation.

items.q: Mammoth Capital runs a serverless trading API on AWS Lambda behind API Gateway. Traders notice that the very first request after an idle period has a 500-millisecond delay, while immediately subsequent requests finish in 15 milliseconds. What causes this initial delay, and what AWS feature prevents it?
opts: Route Table propagation lag; fix it by moving Lambda into a public subnet with an Elastic IP.
Deployment package corruption; fix it by zipping the function under 50 MB.
Soft concurrency throttling at 1,000 requests; fix it by switching from API Gateway to S3 triggers.
A Lambda cold start while AWS initializes the execution environment; fix it by enabling Provisioned Concurrency (or scheduled warm-up pings).
items.exp: When a Lambda function has not been invoked recently, AWS must initialize a new execution environment, causing a 100ms–1s cold start delay. Enabling Provisioned Concurrency pre-warms the function (at an added cost) to eliminate cold starts.

items.q: Whenever a client uploads a trade confirmation file to an Amazon S3 bucket, Mammoth Capital wants a Python function to run for roughly 312 milliseconds, parse the file, store the result in DynamoDB, and incur zero compute charges while idle. Which setup fits best?
opts: A dedicated bare metal EC2 instance polling the S3 bucket every second.
An On-Demand EC2 instance running 24/7 with an attached EBS volume.
An AWS Lambda function triggered directly by an S3 PUT event.
A 3-year Reserved EC2 instance running a cron job every hour.
items.exp: An S3 PUT event can directly trigger an AWS Lambda function to process the uploaded file and write to DynamoDB, billing only for the 312 milliseconds of execution and zero while idle.

items.q: Mammoth Capital wants to commit to a 3-year reservation for its core EC2 fleet, but the engineering team expects their needs to evolve next year and wants the option to exchange their reservation for a different instance family or type. Which Reserved Instance flavor should they choose?
opts: Convertible Reserved Instances, which offer a slightly smaller discount than Standard RIs in exchange for the ability to swap instance types or families.
Standard Reserved Instances, which provide the deepest discount and allow free exchanges across any instance family at any time.
Spot Instances, which lock in capacity for 3 years with a 90% discount and zero interruptions.
On-Demand Instances, which automatically convert into a 72% discount after 12 months.
items.exp: Standard RIs lock you into one specific instance type for the deepest discount, whereas Convertible RIs trade a slightly smaller discount for the flexibility to exchange for a different instance type or family as your needs evolve.
items.topic: EC2 Cost Optimization: Reserved, Spot & Savings Plans

items.q: Instead of reserving specific EC2 instance types, Mammoth Capital's FinOps team wants to commit to a minimum dollar spend per hour (for example, $5.00/hr) and have AWS automatically apply the discount across their highest-cost EC2, Lambda, and Fargate usage. Which model works this way?
opts: Standard Reserved Instances
EC2 Spot Instances
AWS Savings Plans
On-Demand Per-Second Billing
items.exp: Savings Plans let you commit to a fixed hourly dollar spend rather than a specific instance type, and AWS automatically applies the discount across EC2, Lambda, and Fargate usage.
items.topic: EC2 Cost Optimization: Reserved, Spot & Savings Plans

items.q: Why should Mammoth Capital never run its stateful production database on an EC2 Spot Instance despite the up to 90% discount?
opts: Spot Instances cannot attach EBS volumes or run inside a VPC.
If AWS needs spare capacity back, it gives a non-negotiable 2-minute warning and terminates the Spot Instance, making Spot suitable only for fault-tolerant, stateless, interruptible workloads.
Spot Instances automatically wipe all S3 buckets in the account when spot prices rise.
Spot Instances require a mandatory 3-year upfront lease commitment.
items.exp: AWS sells spare capacity as Spot Instances at up to 90% off, but if AWS needs that capacity back, it terminates the instance after a 2-minute warning—ideal for stateless batch processing or ML training, never for a production database.
items.topic: EC2 Cost Optimization: Reserved, Spot & Savings Plans

items.q: Mammoth Capital is deploying a 150-node Apache Kafka cluster across three Availability Zones to ingest real-time market feeds. The architecture must ensure that a single hardware rack failure in an AZ cannot take down more than one replication group of brokers. Which placement strategy should they use?
opts: Cluster Placement Group
Spread Placement Group
Partition Placement Group
Dedicated Hosts in a single AZ
items.exp: A Spread Placement Group is capped at 7 instances per AZ (max 21 across 3 AZs), so it cannot hold 150 nodes. A Partition Placement Group isolates instances into rack-independent partitions and scales to hundreds of instances for topology-aware systems like Kafka and HDFS.

items.q: A quantitative research team runs tightly coupled fluid-dynamics and pricing simulations using Message Passing Interface (MPI) on Linux EC2 instances. They need the lowest possible inter-node latency and OS-bypass networking. Which combination should they configure?
opts: Cluster Placement Group with Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA)
Spread Placement Group with Elastic Network Adapter (ENA)
Partition Placement Group with secondary Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs)
Multi-AZ Auto Scaling Group with Elastic IPs
items.exp: EFA provides OS-bypass networking specifically built for MPI and HPC workloads on Linux, and pairing it with a Cluster Placement Group places instances in the same AZ on high-bisection-bandwidth racks.

items.q: A risk-modeling EC2 instance takes 18 minutes on boot to load a 64 GB reference dataset into RAM before it can serve requests. The team wants to stop the instance overnight to save compute costs and resume it in under a minute each morning with its memory intact. What must be configured to use EC2 Hibernation?
opts: Attach an Instance Store volume to hold the RAM state
Ensure the root EBS volume is encrypted and has sufficient free space to store the contents of RAM
Place the instance in a Cluster Placement Group with ENA enabled
Convert the instance to a Spot Instance with a persistent request
items.exp: EC2 Hibernation writes the in-memory RAM state to a file on the root EBS volume before shutting down. Because RAM can contain sensitive data, AWS requires the root EBS volume to be encrypted and big enough to hold the RAM dump.

items.q: Mammoth Capital needs to store petabytes of historical MSTR trading data. It's rarely accessed but must be retrieved within 12 hours if needed for audits. What is the most cost-effective S3 class?
opts: S3 Standard
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
items.exp: Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest and provides a retrieval time of 12 hours, perfectly matching the audit requirement. Flexible Retrieval is 1-5 mins or 3-5 hours.

items.q: Which block storage service is best for the boot volume of an EC2 instance running Mammoth's trading bots?
opts: EFS
Instance Store
EBS
S3
items.exp: Elastic Block Store (EBS) provides persistent block storage volumes for use with EC2 instances. Instance Store is ephemeral, EFS is file storage, S3 is object storage.

items.q: Mammoth needs a shared file system that can be mounted concurrently by hundreds of EC2 instances running risk simulations across multiple AZs. What service is designed for this?
opts: EBS Multi-Attach
EFS
S3
Storage Gateway
items.exp: Elastic File System (EFS) is a fully managed NFS file system designed to be shared across thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AZs. EBS Multi-Attach is limited to one AZ and specific instance types.

items.q: Mammoth Capital is deploying an I/O-hungry production database (similar to Oracle RAC or SAP HANA) on EC2 that requires consistent performance of 150,000 IOPS. Which EBS volume type is engineered for this requirement?
opts: sc1 (Cold HDD)
st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD)
gp3 (General Purpose SSD)
io2 Block Express (Provisioned IOPS SSD, supporting up to 256,000 IOPS)
items.exp: io2 Block Express (Provisioned IOPS SSD) delivers up to 256,000 IOPS and is the premium EBS volume type for production databases requiring consistent, high IOPS beyond what gp3 can deliver.

items.q: An engineer has an EC2 instance in us-east-1a with an attached EBS volume. When that AZ experiences an issue, they launch a replacement EC2 instance in us-east-1b and try to attach the existing EBS volume directly to it, but AWS refuses. Why, and what is the protection mechanism to move or restore it across AZs?
opts: EBS volumes are locked to a single Availability Zone; you must create an EBS Snapshot (stored redundantly in S3 across AZs) and restore a new volume from it in us-east-1b.
EBS volumes can only attach to instances in different Regions, not different Availability Zones in the same Region.
Only sc1 Cold HDD volumes can cross Availability Zones; gp3 volumes cannot be backed up.
You must mount S3 directly as a block boot volume on the instance in us-east-1b.
items.exp: An EBS volume is locked to the single Availability Zone where it was created. Taking an EBS Snapshot copies the volume's contents redundantly into S3 across AZs, allowing you to restore a volume in any AZ or Region.

items.q: Mammoth Capital runs a log-processing and data-warehouse node on EC2 that reads large files sequentially rather than randomly and needs low-cost, high-throughput sequential disk reads. Which EBS volume type fits best?
opts: io2 Block Express (Provisioned IOPS SSD)
gp3 with maximum random IOPS
st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD)
EBS Multi-Attach io1 across three Regions
items.exp: st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) provides low-cost, high-throughput sequential read/write access ideal for big data, log processing, and data warehouses that stream large files sequentially.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's portal generates resized image thumbnails from original user uploads stored in S3. The thumbnails are accessed less than once a month, need millisecond retrieval when requested, and can easily be recreated if an Availability Zone has an outage. Which S3 storage class minimizes cost?
opts: S3 Standard
S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
items.exp: S3 One Zone-IA offers millisecond retrieval at 20% lower cost than Standard-IA by storing data in a single AZ, making it ideal for infrequently accessed, reproducible data like thumbnails.

items.q: Mammoth Capital archives quarterly compliance reports that are accessed only once per quarter, but when a compliance officer clicks a report, it must open in milliseconds rather than waiting minutes or hours. Which S3 storage class is built for this middle ground?
opts: S3 Glacier Deep Archive (12-hour retrieval)
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (1 minute to 12 hours retrieval)
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (archive pricing with millisecond retrieval)
S3 Standard (most expensive per GB stored)
items.exp: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval provides archive-level storage pricing while maintaining millisecond retrieval speed, specifically designed for data accessed roughly once per quarter.

items.q: Server logs at Mammoth Capital are actively debugged for the first 30 days, rarely checked between 30 and 90 days, kept for 7 years (2,555 days) for legal audits, and then deleted. What S3 feature automates moving these logs across storage classes and deleting them on schedule?
opts: S3 Lifecycle Policies configured with transition and expiration rules
S3 Block Public Access rules
Manual monthly EBS Snapshot copies
S3 Pre-Signed URLs with a 7-year TTL
items.exp: S3 Lifecycle Policies let you define automated rules that transition aging objects from S3 Standard to Standard-IA and Glacier tiers, and automatically delete them after 2,555 days (7 years).

items.q: A developer mistakenly attaches an S3 Bucket Policy containing "Allow public read" to Mammoth Capital's confidential bucket. However, S3 Block Public Access is enabled on the bucket and account. What happens when someone on the internet tries to read an object?
opts: The request succeeds because an explicit Allow in a Bucket Policy overrides Block Public Access.
The request succeeds for existing objects but fails for new uploads.
The request succeeds if legacy Object ACLs are also enabled.
The request is blocked because S3 Block Public Access is the master override that supersedes all Bucket Policies and ACLs that would make data public.
items.exp: S3 Block Public Access acts as a master lockdown switch at the account or bucket level, overriding any Bucket Policy, ACL, or object permission that would otherwise expose data publicly.
items.topic: S3 Security: Bucket Policies, ACLs & Pre-Signed URLs

items.q: Mammoth Capital stores private client invoice PDFs in S3. When an authenticated client clicks "Download Invoice" in the web app, they need access to their specific PDF for 24 hours without making the bucket public or creating IAM Users for external clients. What is the standard pattern?
opts: Create an IAM User for every client and email them long-term access keys.
Have the backend generate an S3 Pre-Signed URL with a 24-hour expiry for that specific object.
Disable S3 Block Public Access on the bucket for 24 hours.
Enable legacy S3 Object ACLs and grant read access to the internet.
items.exp: An S3 Pre-Signed URL is a time-limited link generated by your backend that grants temporary access to one specific private object and expires automatically after its TTL (such as 24 hours).
items.topic: S3 Security: Bucket Policies, ACLs & Pre-Signed URLs

items.q: An IAM Role in AWS Account A needs to read objects from an S3 bucket in AWS Account B. How do IAM Policies and S3 Bucket Policies interact in a cross-account scenario versus a same-account scenario?
opts: In both same-account and cross-account access, only legacy ACLs are evaluated.
Same-account access requires both the IAM Policy and Bucket Policy to allow the action, whereas cross-account access requires only one.
For same-account access, either an IAM Policy OR a Bucket Policy granting access is sufficient; for cross-account access, BOTH must allow the action.
Cross-account S3 access is impossible without making the bucket public.
items.exp: Within the same AWS account, permission in either the identity's IAM Policy or the resource's S3 Bucket Policy is enough, but for cross-account access, both policies must explicitly allow the action.
items.topic: S3 Security: Bucket Policies, ACLs & Pre-Signed URLs

items.q: Mammoth Capital stores 200 TB of raw equity tick data in Amazon S3. Their quantitative researchers run a Linux-based HPC cluster on EC2 that needs to process this data as a POSIX file system at hundreds of gigabytes per second during 6-hour simulation runs, then write the output back to S3. Which storage service should they use?
opts: Amazon EFS with Lifecycle Management enabled
Amazon FSx for Lustre integrated with the S3 bucket
Amazon EBS io2 Block Express with Multi-Attach
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
items.exp: FSx for Lustre is purpose-built for Linux HPC workloads requiring massive parallel throughput and native bidirectional integration with Amazon S3.

items.q: A company runs 40 Linux EC2 instances across three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. All instances need concurrent read/write access to uploaded user documents, and documents older than 60 days are rarely accessed. Which solution provides shared storage at the lowest cost?
opts: Use Amazon EFS Standard with a Lifecycle Policy to transition files to EFS Infrequent Access (EFS-IA) after 60 days
Attach a gp3 EBS volume to all 40 instances across the three AZs
Deploy Amazon FSx for Lustre Scratch file systems in each AZ
Use Amazon S3 mounted directly as a block device on each EC2 instance
items.exp: EFS is a Multi-AZ NFS file system for Linux that thousands of EC2 instances can mount concurrently, and EFS Lifecycle Management automatically moves cold files to EFS-IA to slash storage costs.

items.q: An enterprise is migrating an on-premises application that requires a single shared storage volume accessible simultaneously by both Windows Server instances (over SMB) and Linux instances (over NFS), while replicating data from their existing on-premises NetApp storage array. Which service fits?
opts: Amazon EFS
Amazon FSx for OpenZFS
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
items.exp: FSx for NetApp ONTAP natively supports multi-protocol access (both NFS and SMB concurrently to the same data) and uses NetApp SnapMirror for seamless replication from on-premises NetApp systems.

items.q: For highly structured, relational financial ledger data that requires complex JOIN operations, which AWS service is best?
opts: DynamoDB
DocumentDB
RDS
Neptune
items.exp: Amazon RDS is a relational database service (SQL) designed for structured data and complex queries (JOINs). DynamoDB is NoSQL, DocumentDB is for JSON, Neptune is a graph database.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's mobile app leaderboard needs to handle millions of reads and writes per second with single-digit millisecond latency. Which database fits this use case?
opts: Aurora
RDS PostgreSQL
DynamoDB
Redshift
items.exp: DynamoDB is a key-value NoSQL database designed for single-digit millisecond performance at any scale, ideal for high-throughput leaderboards. Aurora/RDS are relational, Redshift is for analytics.

items.q: To improve the read performance of their RDS database during peak trading hours, Mammoth should deploy:
opts: Multi-AZ Deployments
Read Replicas
ElastiCache
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
items.exp: Read Replicas allow you to offload read traffic from the primary database instance, improving read performance. Multi-AZ is for high availability (disaster recovery), not performance.

items.q: Mammoth Capital is launching a new market-alert feature whose traffic is spiky and unpredictable—quiet for hours, then surging to hundreds of thousands of writes per second on breaking news. Which DynamoDB throughput mode scales automatically and bills per request?
opts: On-Demand mode
Provisioned mode with fixed Read and Write Capacity Units
SQL Connection Pooler mode
RDS Synchronous Standby mode
items.exp: DynamoDB On-Demand mode scales automatically to handle unpredictable or spiky traffic and bills per request, whereas Provisioned mode requires specifying Read and Write Capacity Units in advance.

items.q: A developer designs a DynamoDB table and picks a Primary Key whose Partition Key has almost no variety, causing 95% of all reads and writes to hit the exact same key value. What performance issue will this poor key design cause, and how does DynamoDB achieve its speed when designed properly?
opts: Connection pool exhaustion, because DynamoDB requires persistent TCP database connections.
A "hot partition" bottleneck; when designed properly, DynamoDB achieves single-digit millisecond latency at any scale via direct Primary Key lookups rather than complex SQL joins or table scans.
Slow SQL JOIN execution across foreign keys.
Schema migration lockups whenever an item adds a new JSON attribute.
items.exp: DynamoDB delivers single-digit millisecond latency from 1 MB to 1 PB by doing direct Primary Key (Partition Key or Partition Key + Sort Key) lookups without joins, so a poorly chosen Partition Key creates a "hot partition" bottleneck.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's trading engine reads reference data from DynamoDB millions of times per second and needs read latency reduced from single-digit milliseconds down to microseconds. What AWS feature sits in front of DynamoDB to do this?
opts: An RDS PostgreSQL Read Replica
A VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3
A composite SQL Foreign Key
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), an in-memory cache for DynamoDB
items.exp: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache that sits in front of DynamoDB and reduces read latency from milliseconds to microseconds for read-heavy workloads.

items.q: Mammoth Capital is building a real-time trading competition leaderboard that requires sorted sets, pub/sub messaging, data persistence that survives a reboot, and Multi-AZ automatic failover. Which ElastiCache engine should they choose?
opts: ElastiCache for Memcached
ElastiCache for Redis
RDS Read Replicas
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
items.exp: ElastiCache for Redis supports persistence across restarts, Multi-AZ replication with automatic failover, pub/sub messaging, and complex data types like sorted sets for leaderboards.
items.topic: ElastiCache: The Caching Layer (Redis vs Memcached)

items.q: When a user requests a page, Mammoth Capital's app checks ElastiCache first. On a cache hit, it returns the data in microseconds; on a cache miss, it queries the database, writes the result to the cache with a TTL, and returns it. What is this pattern called, and when would you pick Memcached over Redis?
opts: Write-Through Sharding; pick Memcached when you need Multi-AZ failover and disk persistence.
Synchronous Failover; pick Memcached when you need geospatial indexing and Lua scripting.
Envelope Caching; pick Memcached when you need to retain compliance data for 7 years.
The Lazy Loading pattern; pick Memcached when you want a pure, simple, multi-threaded object cache and can tolerate losing the cache on restart.
items.exp: Checking the cache first and populating it with a TTL on a cache miss is the Lazy Loading pattern. Memcached is a pure, multi-threaded object cache chosen when you want raw caching simplicity without persistence or replication.
items.topic: ElastiCache: The Caching Layer (Redis vs Memcached)

items.q: Mammoth Capital's RDS database CPU is at 90% because 50,000 users are simultaneously requesting the exact same market summary page, running identical read queries for data that hasn't changed in the last 30 seconds. What is the best first recommendation?
opts: Add an Amazon ElastiCache layer in front of the database so repeated requests are served from memory in microseconds without hitting RDS.
Enable RDS Multi-AZ so the standby instance processes half of the read queries.
Deploy an RDS Read Replica so the exact same query can still run 50,000 times across two servers.
Move the RDS database into a public subnet.
items.exp: Unlike a Read Replica—which still executes the query on a database—ElastiCache eliminates repeated queries entirely by serving the cached result from memory in microseconds, dropping database load by ~90%.
items.topic: ElastiCache: The Caching Layer (Redis vs Memcached)

items.q: Mammoth Capital migrated an order-status API from EC2 to AWS Lambda backed by an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database. During market open, thousands of concurrent Lambda executions launch simultaneously, causing 'too many connections' errors on the database. What is the most operationally efficient fix?
opts: Deploy Amazon RDS Proxy between the Lambda functions and the RDS database
Enable Multi-AZ on the RDS database to double the connection limit
Place an Application Load Balancer between the Lambda functions and RDS
Migrate the relational schema and SQL JOIN queries into Amazon S3
items.exp: RDS Proxy pools and multiplexes database connections from stateless, rapidly scaling compute like AWS Lambda, preventing connection exhaustion and speeding up failover.

items.q: A global financial compliance requirement states that Mammoth Capital's relational PostgreSQL database must survive a complete AWS Region outage with a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) of under 1 second and a Recovery Time Objective (RTO) of under 1 minute. Which architecture satisfies this?
opts: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL with a Multi-AZ deployment
Amazon RDS PostgreSQL with automated snapshots copied across Regions every 5 minutes
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Global Database
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 in a single Region
items.exp: Aurora Global Database uses storage-layer replication across Regions with sub-second lag (RPO < 1s) and can promote a secondary Region to full read/write in under 1 minute (RTO < 1m).

items.q: How does Amazon Aurora achieve high durability and fast read replica scaling within a single Region compared to standard Amazon RDS?
opts: Each Aurora Read Replica maintains its own independent EBS gp3 volume synchronized via nightly snapshots
Aurora separates compute from storage, writing 6 copies of data across 3 Availability Zones in a shared storage volume used by both the primary and up to 15 replicas
Aurora stores all database tables in instance store NVMe drives and backs them up to Glacier
Aurora uses DynamoDB tables under the hood and translates SQL queries at runtime
items.exp: Aurora decouples compute and storage, automatically maintaining 6 copies across 3 AZs in a shared cluster volume. All up to 15 Aurora Replicas read from that same shared storage, keeping lag to milliseconds and allowing any replica to act as a failover target.

items.q: Mammoth Capital's web application receives HTTP/HTTPS traffic. They need to route traffic based on the URL path (e.g., /api vs /web). Which load balancer should they use?
opts: Application Load Balancer (ALB)
Network Load Balancer (NLB)
Classic Load Balancer (CLB)
Gateway Load Balancer (GLB)
items.exp: The ALB operates at Layer 7 and supports advanced routing features like path-based and host-based routing. NLB is Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), GLB is for virtual appliances.

items.q: Which service automatically adjusts the number of EC2 instances in response to changing demand, ensuring Mammoth always has enough compute for their algos?
opts: Elastic Load Balancing
Auto Scaling Groups
Route 53
CloudWatch Alarms
items.exp: Auto Scaling Groups (ASG) automatically add (scale out) or remove (scale in) EC2 instances based on defined policies or metrics.

items.q: To ensure high availability of their database, Mammoth deployed RDS across two Availability Zones. This feature is known as:
opts: Read Replicas
Multi-AZ Deployment
Global Database
Active-Active Architecture
items.exp: Multi-AZ Deployment creates a synchronous standby replica in a different AZ for failover purposes. It is for HA, not performance.

items.q: When a user uploads a file to S3 at Mammoth Capital, that single event must trigger three parallel pipelines: thumbnail generation, content moderation, and search indexing. Each service must process items at its own pace with zero message loss even if a consumer is temporarily down. What is the canonical architecture?
opts: Send the S3 event to a single SQS queue shared by all three services.
Have S3 call three EC2 instances directly over HTTP with no queueing.
The SNS-to-SQS Fan-Out pattern: publish the S3 event to an SNS Topic that fans out copies to three separate SQS queues, one per service.
Store the event in local EC2 memory and have each service poll via SSH.
items.exp: In the SNS -> SQS Fan-Out pattern, SNS pushes a copy of the single event to all three subscribed SQS queues simultaneously, and each SQS queue durably retains its messages (up to 14 days) so each service can pull at its own pace.

items.q: A junior developer asks why SNS and SQS have different delivery models and what happens if an endpoint is offline when a message is sent. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: SNS is pull-based and holds messages for 14 days, whereas SQS is push-based and drops messages if a consumer is offline.
SNS is push-based (delivers immediately to subscribers, losing the message if a non-queue subscriber is offline), whereas SQS is pull-based (consumers poll the queue and messages wait up to 14 days).
