items.q: Mammoth Capital's team over-provisioned 200 m5.2xlarge EC2 instances at launch, and CloudWatch now shows 4% average CPU utilization. What should the company do FIRST before purchasing any 3-year Reserved Instances or Savings Plans?
opts: Commit all 200 m5.2xlarge instances to a 3-year Standard Reserved Instance immediately.
Convert the production database to Spot Instances without checking metrics.
Disable CloudWatch metrics to cut monitoring expenses.
Use AWS Compute Optimizer and CloudWatch metrics to analyze usage patterns and right-size the instances (for example, downsizing from m5.2xlarge to m5.large) before committing.
items.exp: Always analyze usage and right-size your fleet before committing to Reserved Instances or Savings Plans; committing to an oversized instance type locks you into paying for unused capacity for 1 to 3 years.

items.q: Once Mammoth Capital's fleet is right-sized, how should the architect choose between EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Compute Savings Plans?
opts: EC2 Instance Savings Plans cover Lambda and Fargate across all Regions, whereas Compute Savings Plans are locked to one family and Region.

EC2 Instance Savings Plans commit to a specific instance family and Region for the deepest discount (up to 72%), whereas Compute Savings Plans commit to $/hour spend and apply flexibly across any EC2 type, Region, OS, plus Lambda and Fargate.
Both plans require bidding on spare EC2 capacity with a 2-minute termination notice.
Compute Savings Plans only apply to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
items.exp: EC2 Instance Savings Plans give the deepest discount (up to 72%) but lock you to a specific instance family and Region, while Compute Savings Plans offer a slightly smaller discount in exchange for full flexibility across any EC2 instance type, Region, OS, Lambda, and Fargate.

items.q: Mammoth Capital has an S3 bucket with uncertain access patterns and also wants Cost Explorer to break down the monthly AWS bill by Project, Environment (prod/staging/dev), and Owner. Which two practices should the architect implement?
opts: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the bucket (to automatically move objects between Standard and IA tiers without retrieval fees) and apply Cost Allocation Tags (Project, Environment, Owner) to all resources.
Move the bucket to S3 One Zone-IA and attach Service Control Policies to Cost Explorer.
Delete all objects after 7 days and use AWS X-Ray annotations for billing reports.
Purchase EC2 Reserved Instances for the S3 bucket and enable S3 Block Public Access.
items.exp: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically shifts objects between Standard and IA tiers based on actual access patterns with no retrieval fees, while Cost Allocation Tags let Cost Explorer break down spending by Project, Environment, and Owner.

items.q: Mammoth Capital runs a fleet of EC2 instances in private subnets that read and write 150 TB of historical market data every month to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region. AWS Cost Explorer reveals thousands of dollars per month in NAT Gateway data processing charges. Which architectural change eliminates these NAT Gateway charges at the lowest cost?
opts: Replace the managed NAT Gateways with self-managed EC2 NAT instances on m6i.4xlarge
Create a Gateway VPC Endpoint for Amazon S3 and add a route to it in the private subnet route tables
Create an Interface VPC Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for Amazon S3
Move the EC2 instances into public subnets and assign Elastic IP addresses to each instance
items.exp: A Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 (and DynamoDB) is completely free ($0/hr and $0/GB) and routes traffic from private subnets directly to S3 over the AWS backbone, bypassing the NAT Gateway entirely.
items.topic: The Hidden Bill: Data Transfer & NAT Costs

items.q: An engineering team runs two high-throughput microservices on EC2 instances within the exact same Availability Zone. They notice unexpected data transfer charges on their monthly AWS bill for traffic between these two microservices. What is the most likely cause?
opts: AWS always charges $0.02/GB for any network traffic between two EC2 instances in the same AZ
They are using a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 in the same VPC
Security Groups charge per gigabyte of stateful packet inspection
The microservices are communicating with each other using their Public IPv4 or Elastic IP addresses instead of their Private IPv4 addresses
items.exp: Data transfer between EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone is free only when using private IP addresses. Communicating via Public or Elastic IPs incurs egress and ingress data transfer charges even within the same AZ.
items.topic: The Hidden Bill: Data Transfer & NAT Costs

items.q: A media company hosts terabytes of downloadable PDF research reports and video briefings on EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in us-east-1 for a global audience. How can they simultaneously reduce EC2 internet data egress costs and improve download speeds for global users?
opts: Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the Application Load Balancer and cache the media assets at edge locations
Enable Cross-Zone Load Balancing on the Application Load Balancer
Route the public internet traffic through an AWS NAT Gateway in each Availability Zone
Switch the Application Load Balancer to a Gateway Load Balancer
items.exp: Data transfer from an AWS origin (like S3 or an ALB) to Amazon CloudFront is free ($0.00/GB), and CloudFront caches assets at 450+ edge locations globally with lower egress pricing and lower latency.
items.topic: The Hidden Bill: Data Transfer & NAT Costs

items.q: Difference between Security Group and NACL?
items.back: Security Groups are stateful, instance-level. NACLs are stateless, subnet-level.
items.analogy: SG is the bouncer at the club door. NACL is the police barricade at the street corner.

items.q: What does Route 53 Failover Routing do?
items.back: Routes traffic to a secondary IP if the primary health check fails.
items.analogy: It's your automated margin call — if the primary account fails, it instantly pivots to the backup.

items.q: Why use Aurora over RDS?
items.back: Aurora scales read replicas faster (milliseconds lag), auto-scales storage, and fails over faster.
items.analogy: RDS is a manual transmission. Aurora is a dual-clutch automatic. You pay a premium so you don't have to shift gears under load.

items.q: What is an SQS Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)?
items.back: A queue for messages that failed to process after multiple attempts.
items.analogy: It's the 'failed trades' ledger. If the order won't clear, don't block the pipe. Move it to the DLQ for manual review.

items.q: Difference between CloudTrail and Config?
items.back: CloudTrail logs WHO made an API call. Config tracks WHAT the state of the resource is.
items.analogy: CloudTrail is the security camera in the server room. Config is the daily inventory checklist.

items.q: Explain the difference between Bare Metal, Virtual Machines, and Containers in one sentence each.
items.back: Bare Metal is an entire physical server dedicated to one OS. A Virtual Machine slices that physical server into multiple isolated fake computers with their own OS. A Container is a lightweight package of code that shares the host's OS kernel, making it instantly bootable.
items.analogy: Bare Metal = you bought a house and live in it alone. VMs = you rent an apartment — shared building, private walls. Containers = shared apartment with thin walls, all tenants use the same stairwell (OS kernel).

items.q: If a lightning strike destroys a data center, how does a Multi-AZ deployment prevent downtime?
items.back: An Availability Zone (AZ) is a physically isolated data center with independent power and networking. A Region contains multiple AZs. If lightning destroys AZ-A, your application automatically shifts traffic to your redundant resources in AZ-B within the same Region.
items.analogy: Multi-AZ is like storing your MSTR trade journal in both Dropbox and a local NAS simultaneously. One burns down, you lose nothing.

items.q: A CTO asks why they shouldn't just buy a bigger server (Vertical Scaling) instead of managing multiple small servers (Horizontal Scaling).
items.back: Vertical Scaling has a hard physical ceiling (you can only buy a server so big) and requires downtime to upgrade. Horizontal Scaling has virtually no ceiling and allows you to dynamically add/remove servers on the fly without interrupting traffic.
items.analogy: Vertical scaling is buying a faster race car for the same single driver. Horizontal scaling is adding more race cars and more drivers. At some point no single car goes fast enough — you need a fleet.

items.q: Your e-commerce site gets a massive traffic spike on Black Friday. How do you survive it without paying for idle servers the rest of the year?
items.back: Use an Auto Scaling Group (ASG). You set rules based on CPU load. When traffic spikes, the ASG automatically provisions new EC2 instances to handle the load. When the spike subsides, it automatically terminates them to stop the billing.
items.analogy: Black Friday traffic is your MSTR earnings call spike. ASG is your trading bot that auto-adds compute when volatility spikes and scales down when it's quiet — you pay for exactly what you used.

items.q: What is an EC2 instance, and what is its primary use case in a modern cloud architecture?
items.back: EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is a standard Virtual Machine in AWS. It is the workhorse of the cloud, used when you need full control over the operating system, need to run legacy applications, or require sustained, uninterrupted compute power for long periods.
items.analogy: EC2 is a virtual machine you rent by the second. Think of it like your Proxmox homelab VM, but running in AWS's datacenter instead of your basement. Same concept — CPU, RAM, disk — just someone else manages the hardware.

items.q: Explain AWS Lambda's pricing model and why it is called 'Serverless'.
items.back: Lambda executes code in response to events without you provisioning or managing any underlying servers (hence 'Serverless'). You are billed purely by the millisecond of execution time. If your code isn't running, you pay absolutely nothing.
items.analogy: Lambda is the vending machine of compute. The machine sits idle (free). When you insert a coin (event), it runs and charges you only for those seconds. Your Proxmox VM charges you 24/7 whether you touch it or not.

items.q: A developer wants to hardcode AWS credentials into their application to access S3. Why is this a fatal flaw, and what is the IAM solution?
items.back: Hardcoded credentials can be leaked in source code or compromised. The correct solution is IAM Roles. You assign an IAM Role to the EC2 instance or Lambda function, which securely requests temporary, rotating credentials from AWS on the fly.
items.analogy: Hardcoding credentials is like tattooing your brokerage password on your arm. IAM Roles are the OAuth token scoped only to what that app needs — no permanent credential, no tattoo to regret.

items.q: Your compliance team mandates that all database backups must be 'Encrypted at Rest'. What AWS service manages this?
items.back: AWS KMS (Key Management Service). KMS handles the creation, rotation, and usage logging of encryption keys. You simply check 'Enable Encryption' on RDS or S3, and AWS uses KMS to transparently encrypt the data before it hits the disk.
items.analogy: Compliance encryption is like sealing your trade records in a fireproof safe only you have the key to. AWS KMS is that key management system — CMK means you own the key, not AWS.

items.q: A competitor launches a DDoS attack against your web application, flooding it with fake HTTP requests. Which service blocks this?
items.back: AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) inspects incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic and blocks malicious payloads (like SQL injection) or rate-limits IPs. For volumetric DDoS attacks (Layer 3/4), AWS Shield automatically mitigates the flood.
items.analogy: DDoS is someone jamming your phone lines so no real customers can get through. Shield Advanced is your enterprise PBX that absorbs the junk calls and keeps legitimate callers connected.

items.q: What is the difference between ECS, EKS, and Fargate?
items.back: ECS is AWS's proprietary container orchestrator. EKS is managed Kubernetes. Fargate is the serverless compute engine for both—it allows you to run containers without managing the underlying EC2 instances.
items.analogy: ECS is AWS's own container orchestrator — like using pfSense directly. EKS is managed Kubernetes — like running pfSense with a commercial support contract. Fargate strips away the servers entirely — you just describe what you want to run and AWS makes it happen.

items.q: A data scientist needs to process 10,000 images overnight using a custom script. Which Compute service is optimized for this?
items.back: AWS Batch. It dynamically provisions the exact quantity and type of compute resources (like GPU instances) needed to chew through a massive queue of batch computing jobs, then spins them down when the queue is empty.
items.analogy: Spot Instances for batch jobs are like buying standby plane tickets at 90% off. If the plane fills up (AWS needs capacity back), you get bumped — but for overnight batch work, that's a fine tradeoff.

items.q: Your Lambda function is in a private subnet with no internet access. It needs to read objects from S3. What do you create, and what does it cost?
items.back: A VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3. It creates a private route inside Amazon's network from your VPC directly to S3, with no internet traversal required. Gateway Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free of charge.
items.analogy: A VPC endpoint is a private back-door from your house directly into the AWS service building. No need to go out the front door onto the public internet just to check your mailbox.

items.q: What is the difference between a VPC Gateway Endpoint and a VPC Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink)?
items.back: Gateway Endpoints are free, route-table-based, and only work with S3 and DynamoDB. Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink) create an ENI with a private IP in your subnet and work with almost all AWS services (SQS, SNS, KMS, etc.) but have an hourly cost.
items.analogy: Gateway Endpoint = a free special on-ramp to the S3 and DynamoDB highways, built directly into your VPC's routing table. Interface Endpoint = a private tunnel using AWS PrivateLink, works with 100+ services but costs per hour.

items.q: A company runs a batch processing workload that is fault-tolerant and can be interrupted. What EC2 pricing model gives up to 90% savings?
items.back: EC2 Spot Instances. AWS sells spare capacity at up to 90% discount. The trade-off: AWS can terminate your instance with a 2-minute warning when they need the capacity back. Only use for fault-tolerant, stateless workloads like data processing, ML training, or rendering.
items.analogy: Fault-tolerant batch jobs on Spot are like running a long render job on your homelab overnight. If a VM crashes, you restart the chunk. You pay 10% of On-Demand because you accepted the interruption risk.

items.q: A company needs production web servers running 24/7 for 3 years. What is the most cost-effective EC2 commitment model?
items.back: Reserved Instances (1 or 3-year term) — up to 72% savings over On-Demand. For flexibility across instance types or regions, Compute Savings Plans offer similar savings without being locked to a specific instance type.
items.analogy: Committing to Reserved Instances for steady workloads is like signing a 3-year office lease instead of paying hotel rates nightly. You get up to 72% off because you gave AWS the certainty they love.

items.q: What is the cheapest S3 storage class for compliance audit logs that must be retained for 7 years and will almost never be accessed?
items.back: S3 Glacier Deep Archive. It offers the lowest storage cost (pennies per TB/month) with retrieval times of up to 12 hours. Use Lifecycle Policies to automatically transition objects there after 90 days.
items.analogy: Glacier Deep Archive is the offsite safety deposit box for data you'll never look at but legally must keep. You pay almost nothing per GB because the retrieval SLA is 12 hours — fine for a regulator's annual audit.

items.q: A media company stores private videos in S3. Authenticated users need temporary access to stream a specific video. What is the correct pattern?
items.back: Generate a Pre-Signed URL using the AWS SDK with a time-limited expiry (e.g., 1 or 24 hours). The URL grants access to exactly one object and self-destructs after the expiry time. The bucket itself remains private at all times.
items.analogy: CloudFront Signed URLs are like temporary VIP wristbands. The S3 bucket stays locked (no public access). When a user pays and authenticates, your server generates a signed URL that works for 24 hours then expires automatically.

items.q: Your RDS database is being hammered by the same read queries from thousands of users. What is the first architectural recommendation to improve performance without a schema change?
items.back: Add an ElastiCache layer (Redis or Memcached) in front of the database. Cache frequently-accessed query results in memory. Cache hits return in microseconds without touching the database. This is the Lazy Loading pattern.
items.analogy: ElastiCache is RAM on steroids sitting in front of your database. The hot queries hit the cache (microseconds); only cache misses hit RDS. Like your browser cache — why reload a page you've already downloaded?

items.q: When would you choose Redis over Memcached for ElastiCache?
items.back: Choose Redis when you need: data persistence (cache survives restarts), replication and Multi-AZ failover, complex data types (sorted sets for leaderboards), or pub/sub messaging. Choose Memcached for pure, simple object caching with no persistence requirements.
items.analogy: Memcached = a simple whiteboard you erase and rewrite. Redis = a whiteboard with undo history, pub/sub messaging, and the ability to sort lists. Pick Redis whenever you need more than a dumb key-value store.

items.q: An order processing system must process orders in the exact sequence they were received, with no duplicates. Which SQS queue type do you use?
items.back: SQS FIFO (First-In-First-Out) Queue. FIFO queues guarantee ordering and exactly-once processing. Note the throughput limit: up to 3,000 messages/second with batching. Standard Queues offer unlimited throughput but only best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery.
items.analogy: SQS FIFO is the velvet rope outside an exclusive club. First in line, first inside. No cutting, no duplicates. Critical for financial transactions where processing a sell order before its corresponding buy would be catastrophic.

items.q: A message in your SQS queue keeps failing processing and crashing the consumer. How do you prevent this from blocking the rest of the queue?
items.back: Configure a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ). After a message fails processing N times (your configured maxReceiveCount), SQS automatically routes it to the DLQ. This isolates the 'poison pill' message and allows the rest of the queue to continue processing. You then investigate and replay the DLQ messages after fixing the bug.
items.analogy: A Dead-Letter Queue is the email 'bounce' folder. Instead of the failed message re-trying forever and jamming your queue, it gets quarantined after N failures so you can inspect it without disrupting live traffic.

items.q: An S3 image upload event needs to simultaneously trigger a thumbnail Lambda, a moderation Lambda, and push a message to an SQS processing queue. What is the architecture?
items.back: SNS Fan-Out pattern. S3 publishes to an SNS Topic on upload. The SNS Topic has three subscribers: the thumbnail Lambda, the moderation Lambda, and the SQS queue. All three receive the event simultaneously. This is the canonical Fan-Out pattern.
items.analogy: SNS fanout is the expediter in a restaurant kitchen — one ticket comes in, they shout the order to every station simultaneously. Lambda, SQS queue, and email all get the notification in parallel, not sequence.

items.q: What is the key difference between SNS and SQS delivery models?
items.back: SNS is push-based (publish once, push to all subscribers simultaneously). SQS is pull-based (consumers poll the queue and process messages at their own pace). SNS does not retain messages — if no subscriber is online, the message is lost. SQS retains messages for up to 14 days.
items.analogy: SQS = a queue where your worker polls (checks the mailbox). SNS = a push service that calls you (your phone rings). SQS workers set their own pace; SNS subscribers get notified instantly the moment a message arrives.

items.q: Your Lambda must connect to RDS. The password must automatically rotate every 30 days without redeployment. Which service do you use?
items.back: AWS Secrets Manager. It natively integrates with RDS, Redshift, and DocumentDB to automatically rotate credentials on a schedule. Your Lambda calls GetSecretValue at runtime — it always receives the current password without any code changes when rotation occurs.
items.analogy: Secrets Manager with automatic rotation is like having your company's locks changed every 30 days automatically. The security team handles it; the Lambda just calls GetSecretValue at runtime and gets today's current key.

items.q: What is the decision rule between Parameter Store SecureString and Secrets Manager?
items.back: Use Parameter Store SecureString for: encrypted configuration values, feature flags, and non-rotating secrets where free tier matters. Use Secrets Manager ($0.40/secret/month) when automatic credential rotation is required — especially for RDS passwords under compliance mandates (SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI-DSS).
items.analogy: Parameter Store SecureString = a combination-locked filing cabinet (you manage the combo). Secrets Manager = a bank vault with an automatic timelock that rotates the combination every month. Use the vault for production credentials.

items.q: A company has EU users that must be routed to EU servers for GDPR compliance, even if a US server has lower latency. Which Route 53 policy applies?
items.back: Geolocation Routing. It routes based on the user's geographic location regardless of latency, making it the correct choice for data sovereignty, GDPR, and regional compliance requirements. Latency-Based routing would route to the fastest server, which might violate data residency laws.
items.analogy: Route 53 Geolocation routing is the digital equivalent of regional offices — European calls route to the Frankfurt office, US calls to New York. Not based on latency, but on legal/compliance geographic requirements.

items.q: A team wants to deploy a new version to 10% of users first, monitoring for errors before a full rollout. Which Route 53 policy enables this?
items.back: Weighted Routing. Set the new version record to weight 10 and the existing version to weight 90. Route 53 will send 10% of traffic to the new version. This is the canonical canary deployment / traffic shifting pattern using DNS.
items.analogy: Weighted routing for canary deploys is like introducing a new trading strategy with 10% of your capital first. If it performs as expected, you gradually increase the allocation. Protects you from deploying a disaster to 100% of users.

items.q: A company wants to be alerted before their monthly AWS bill exceeds $500. Which service do you configure?
items.back: AWS Budgets. You create a budget with a $500 monthly threshold. AWS sends SNS alerts (email/SMS) when actual or forecasted spend reaches 80%, 90%, and 100% of the budget. Budgets can also trigger automated actions like stopping EC2 instances.
items.analogy: AWS Budgets are your financial circuit breaker. Like a stop-loss order on a trade — you define the threshold and get alerted before it's too late to course-correct.

items.q: A solutions architect reviews the account and finds EC2 instances averaging 3% CPU utilization. What AWS tool recommends the correct right-sized instance type?
items.back: AWS Compute Optimizer. It analyzes historical CloudWatch metrics and uses machine learning to recommend the optimal instance type and size. It also analyzes Lambda memory and ECS task CPU/memory to reduce waste.
items.analogy: Idle EC2 instances burning money are like leaving all the lights on in a building you're not using. Trusted Advisor is the automated janitor that walks the building and says 'these lights have been on for 30 days and nobody's home.'

items.q: Step Functions vs. chaining Lambdas directly?
items.back: Step Functions orchestrates a defined multi-step workflow with built-in retries, branching, and a visual audit trail. Chained Lambdas have none of that — just brittle custom code.
items.analogy: Chained Lambdas are sticky notes passed hand to hand hoping nobody drops one. Step Functions is a project manager tracking every step on a whiteboard.

items.q: Can you install an ACM public certificate directly on an EC2 instance?
items.back: No. ACM public certificates only attach to ALB/NLB, CloudFront, and API Gateway — not directly to an EC2 instance's OS.
items.analogy: ACM certs are keys that only fit the locks on the front gate (load balancer/CDN), not every door inside the building (individual EC2 instances).

items.q: CloudWatch vs. X-Ray — what's the core difference?
items.back: CloudWatch shows aggregated health per service (metrics, logs, alarms). X-Ray traces one specific request end-to-end across every service it touched.
items.analogy: CloudWatch is the airport's overall on-time percentage. X-Ray is one passenger's full boarding-to-landing trace showing exactly which layover ran long.

items.q: What permissions are needed for Account B to read an SSE-KMS encrypted S3 object in Account A?
items.back: Requires a KMS Customer Managed Key (not aws/s3) and four permissions: Account A's S3 bucket policy must allow Account B, Account A's KMS key policy must allow Account B, and Account B's IAM identity policy must allow both s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt.
items.analogy: At Mammoth Capital, the compliance vault door (S3 bucket policy) lets an outside auditor in, but the locked briefcase inside still needs a separate key sign-off (KMS CMK policy).

items.q: GuardDuty vs. Inspector vs. Macie: how do their security scopes differ?
items.back: GuardDuty analyzes logs (CloudTrail, VPC Flow, DNS, EKS) for malicious runtime threats. Inspector continuously scans EC2, ECR container images, and Lambda code for software CVEs and network exposure. Macie scans S3 buckets using ML to detect sensitive data and PII.
items.analogy: In your homelab, GuardDuty watches firewall and auth logs for intruders, Inspector runs apt vulnerability scans on Ubuntu containers, and Macie greps your NAS shares for exposed tax PDFs.

items.q: Cognito User Pool vs. Cognito Identity Pool: when do you use each?
items.back: User Pools handle authentication (sign-up, sign-in, MFA, SAML/OIDC federation) and issue JWT tokens. Identity Pools handle authorization, exchanging a valid identity token for temporary AWS STS credentials so clients can directly call AWS services like S3 or DynamoDB.
items.analogy: At Mammoth Capital, the User Pool is lobby security checking your passport and issuing a badge (JWT); the Identity Pool is the trading desk trading that badge for a temporary terminal login (STS).

items.q: Is AWS Direct Connect encrypted by default, and how do you encrypt traffic over it?
items.back: No—Direct Connect is a dedicated private fiber circuit, not encrypted by default. To encrypt traffic in transit, run an AWS Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec) over a public or transit VIF, or enable Direct Connect MACsec (Layer 2 encryption) on supported 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps connections.
items.analogy: Direct Connect is a dedicated dark-fiber line into Mammoth Capital's rack—private, not scrambled. Running Site-to-Site VPN over it is layering a Tailscale WireGuard tunnel over your private VLAN.

items.q: How do you serve private S3 content through CloudFront while blocking direct S3 bucket access?
items.back: Configure CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC, replacing legacy OAI), keep S3 Block Public Access enabled, and attach an S3 bucket policy allowing s3:GetObject only to the CloudFront service principal conditioned on your specific distribution ARN.
items.analogy: Mammoth Capital's research portal serves PDFs through a front-desk receptionist (CloudFront); the back-room vault (S3) only opens for that receptionist's badge (OAC), never for walk-ins.

items.q: Why prefer AWS Systems Manager Session Manager over a Bastion Host for private EC2 shell access?
items.back: Session Manager requires zero inbound security group ports (no port 22), no public IP or jump box to patch, and no SSH keys to manage. Access is gated by IAM policies over an outbound HTTPS agent connection, and every shell command can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3.
items.analogy: A Bastion Host is port-forwarding SSH on your router to a jump VM; Session Manager is like Tailscale SSH—outbound-only agent tunnel, zero open inbound ports, and full audit logging.

items.q: When must you choose a KMS Customer Managed Key (CMK) over an AWS Managed Key?
items.back: Choose a CMK when you need custom key policies, cross-account access, manual on-demand rotation, the ability to disable or schedule deletion of the key, or imported key material (BYOK). AWS Managed Keys (like aws/s3) have locked policies and cannot be shared cross-account.
items.analogy: An AWS Managed Key is the broker's omnibus lock—safe, but they own the policy. A CMK is Mammoth Capital's own vault policy where compliance dictates which subsidiary accounts can decrypt.

items.q: AWS KMS vs. AWS CloudHSM: when does an architecture require CloudHSM?
items.back: KMS is a multi-tenant managed service that integrates natively with AWS storage and databases. Choose CloudHSM only when strict compliance mandates single-tenant dedicated FIPS 140-3 Level 3 hardware under your exclusive control, or custom PKCS#11/JCE cryptographic acceleration.
items.analogy: KMS is a high-security safe deposit box inside a shared Swiss bank; CloudHSM is bolting your own physical HSM appliance into your Proxmox rack where not even the landlord has a key.

items.q: What capabilities does AWS Network Firewall add beyond Security Groups and NACLs?
items.back: Security Groups and NACLs only filter by IP, port, and protocol. AWS Network Firewall adds stateful deep packet inspection (DPI), Suricata-compatible intrusion prevention (IPS) rules, outbound domain/FQDN allow-listing, and centralized inspection across a VPC or Transit Gateway.
items.analogy: SG and NACLs are basic iptables port blocks; AWS Network Firewall is running Suricata IDS/IPS and outbound domain filtering on your homelab pfSense router to inspect packet payloads.

items.q: IAM Permission Boundary vs. AWS Organizations SCP: how do their scopes differ?
items.back: Both act as maximum permission guardrails that never grant access on their own. An SCP applies to an entire AWS account or OU (restricting all principals including member root). A Permission Boundary attaches to a specific IAM user or role, often used to safely delegate role creation.
items.analogy: An SCP is Mammoth Capital's firm-wide risk limit on an entire trading subsidiary; a Permission Boundary is a junior quant's personal position cap so any bot they spin up stays within bounds.

items.q: Does a Service Control Policy (SCP) restrict a member account's root user or the management account?
items.back: An SCP restricts every IAM user, role, and even the root user inside any member account it applies to. However, SCPs never affect principals inside the AWS Organizations management account.
items.analogy: Mammoth Capital's subsidiary compliance rules bind even the subsidiary CEO (member root user), but the parent holding company boardroom (management account) is exempt from subsidiary guardrails.

items.q: S3 Object Lock Governance mode vs. Compliance mode: what is the difference?
items.back: Both enforce WORM (Write Once, Read Many) protection on versioned S3 buckets. In Governance mode, principals with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission can delete or alter locked objects. In Compliance mode, nobody—not even the root user—can delete or shorten retention until it expires.
items.analogy: Governance mode is a read-only ZFS snapshot that root can still destroy with sudo; Compliance mode is SEC trade blotters burned onto physical WORM optical discs locked in a time-lock vault.

items.q: What IP serves EC2 Instance Metadata, and how does IMDSv2 block SSRF credential theft?
items.back: EC2 Instance Metadata is served at link-local IP 169.254.169.254. While IMDSv1 responds to simple GET requests (vulnerable to SSRF), IMDSv2 requires a session-oriented PUT request with a custom TTL header to mint a secret token first, blocking typical SSRF attacks and container hops.
items.analogy: IMDSv1 is an internal homelab status page any tricked web proxy can curl; IMDSv2 forces the caller to first handshake for a short-lived CSRF token before handing over IAM role credentials.

items.q: Which AWS Region must hold an ACM certificate for CloudFront, and which ACM certs auto-renew?
items.back: For CloudFront, the AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate must always reside in us-east-1 (N. Virginia); for ALB or Regional API Gateway, it must match the resource's Region. Public ACM certs validated via DNS (CNAME) auto-renew while attached; imported third-party certs do not.
items.analogy: CloudFront only checks the master keyring in the Virginia headquarters (us-east-1), and ACM only auto-renews keys it forged itself—if you import your own cert, you track expiry yourself.

items.q: What traffic metadata do VPC Flow Logs capture, and what internal VPC traffic is excluded?
items.back: VPC Flow Logs capture IP header metadata (source/dest IP, ports, protocol, byte counts, ACCEPT/REJECT)—never packet payloads. They exclude traffic to 169.254.169.254 (metadata), 169.254.169.123 (Amazon Time Sync), DHCP requests, and queries to the default VPC DNS resolver.
items.analogy: VPC Flow Logs are NetFlow call logs on your router—recording who dialed whom and whether the firewall dropped it, but never recording the phone audio or internal NTP clock checks.

items.q: In IAM policy evaluation, what happens when one policy has an explicit Allow and another has an explicit Deny?
items.back: An explicit Deny always overrides every Allow. AWS starts at an implicit Deny, checks all applicable policies (SCPs, resource policies, permission boundaries, identity and session policies) for any explicit Deny, and grants access only if required Allows exist and zero explicit Denies match.
items.analogy: On Mammoth Capital's trading desk, three portfolio managers can click 'Approve Order,' but if the compliance engine fires a single explicit 'Deny,' the trade is blocked cold.

items.q: How do S3 encryption modes SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, and SSE-C differ in key management?
items.back: SSE-S3 (AES-256, enabled by default) uses keys fully managed by S3. SSE-KMS uses AWS KMS keys, adding CloudTrail key-usage audit logs, key policies, and KMS API rate limits. SSE-C requires the client to send the raw encryption key on every HTTPS request; AWS never stores the key.
items.analogy: SSE-S3 is the building locking your door automatically; SSE-KMS logs every badge swipe in a compliance ledger; SSE-C means you bring your own physical padlock key on every single request.

items.q: Aurora Global Database vs. RDS cross-Region Read Replica: when do you choose Aurora Global Database?
items.back: Aurora Global Database replicates at the storage layer across Regions with typical sub-second lag, zero impact on database compute, and ~1-minute cross-Region DR failover. Standard RDS cross-Region read replicas use asynchronous engine-level replication with higher lag and slower promotion.
items.analogy: RDS cross-Region replication is emailing trade ledgers to London after commits; Aurora Global Database is mirroring raw NVMe blocks over dedicated fiber so London is under a second behind New York.

items.q: VPC Peering vs. AWS Transit Gateway: when do you switch from Peering to Transit Gateway?
items.back: VPC Peering creates a non-transitive 1-to-1 link (ideal for 2–4 VPCs with non-overlapping CIDRs). Transit Gateway acts as a regional hub-and-spoke cloud router supporting transitive routing across dozens or hundreds of VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect links from one central route table.
items.analogy: VPC Peering is running direct crossover cables between two Proxmox hosts; Transit Gateway is installing a central L3 core switch when your homelab scales to 20 isolated VLANs.

items.q: Pilot Light vs. Warm Standby: how do these two AWS Disaster Recovery strategies differ?
items.back: In Pilot Light, only the core stateful data tier (such as an RDS database replica) runs 24/7 in the DR Region while compute instances remain stopped or unprovisioned until failover. In Warm Standby, a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the entire stack runs 24/7 and scales out on failover.
items.analogy: Pilot Light is syncing ZFS snapshots to a backup Proxmox node with the VMs powered off; Warm Standby is running those backup VMs live on 1 vCPU each, ready to scale up if the main rack dies.

items.q: Thousands of concurrent Lambda invocations are exhausting RDS database connections. What is the fix?
items.back: Deploy Amazon RDS Proxy between Lambda and RDS. RDS Proxy pools and reuses established database connections across transient Lambda environments, protects the database from connection storms, and speeds up Multi-AZ failovers by up to 66% by holding client connections while switching primaries.
items.analogy: Without RDS Proxy, 1,000 Lambdas are 1,000 trading bots opening raw TCP sockets to Postgres at once; RDS Proxy is a connection multiplexor funnelling all those bots through 20 warm database pipes.

items.q: AWS Backup vs. Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM): when do you choose AWS Backup?
items.back: DLM only automates schedules for EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs. Choose AWS Backup for centralized, cross-service backup policies across EC2, EBS, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, S3, and Storage Gateway, or when you need Backup Vault Lock (WORM), cross-Region copy, or cross-account vaults.
items.analogy: DLM is a cron script snapping local VM disks; AWS Backup is a central Proxmox Backup Server managing every VM, NAS share, and database across accounts with immutable ransomware protection.

items.q: Amazon EventBridge vs. Amazon SNS: when do you choose EventBridge over SNS?
items.back: SNS is simple, high-throughput pub/sub fan-out. Choose EventBridge when you need content-based routing rules on deep JSON fields, event schema discovery, archive and replay of past events, native SaaS partner event buses (Datadog, Shopify, Auth0), or scheduled cron triggers across AWS services.
items.analogy: SNS is a trading floor PA loudspeaker shouting every fill to all listeners; EventBridge is a smart router inspecting the JSON ticket and sending only 'MSTR block trades > $1M' to the risk engine.

items.q: RDS Multi-AZ DB Instance vs. RDS Multi-AZ DB Cluster: how do they differ?
items.back: A Multi-AZ DB Instance keeps one synchronous standby in a second AZ purely for failover—the standby cannot serve read traffic. A Multi-AZ DB Cluster deploys one writer and two readable standby instances across three AZs using local storage, providing faster failover (~35s) and extra read capacity.
items.analogy: A Multi-AZ DB Instance is a silent understudy who never goes on stage unless the lead actor faints; a Multi-AZ DB Cluster puts two backup actors on stage answering read questions between scenes.

items.q: How do you prevent an Auto Scaling Group from terminating an instance that is mid-way through a long job?
items.back: Use ASG Instance Scale-In Protection (so the worker marks itself protected while busy) or an ASG Terminating Lifecycle Hook, which pauses termination in a Terminating:Wait state (up to 48 hours or until CompleteLifecycleAction is called) so the instance can finish draining active jobs cleanly.
items.analogy: A Terminating Lifecycle Hook is telling a trader 'Pack your desk after your open orders settle' instead of yanking their power cord mid-execution when market volume slows down.

items.q: Define RPO (Recovery Point Objective) vs. RTO (Recovery Time Objective).
items.back: RPO is the maximum acceptable age of lost data measured in time (e.g., RPO of 15 minutes means backups must occur at least every 15 minutes). RTO is the maximum acceptable service downtime between a disaster striking and the application returning to operational status.
items.analogy: When Mammoth Capital's order gateway crashes at 10:15 AM, RPO asks 'How many minutes of trades since the last snapshot did we lose?' while RTO asks 'How long until we're taking orders again?'

items.q: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) vs. AWS DMS: what does each migrate?
items.back: AWS MGN is the primary lift-and-shift (rehost) service for physical, VMware, or cloud servers: it continuously replicates disks at the block level and launches cutover EC2 instances. AWS DMS (Database Migration Service) migrates databases with live change data capture (CDC) and optional engine conversion.
items.analogy: MGN clones an entire Ubuntu VM disk block-for-block from your Proxmox server into EC2; DMS streams live SQL transactions from an on-prem Oracle database into Aurora PostgreSQL.

items.q: What are the default and maximum limits for SQS Visibility Timeout, Message Retention, and Long Polling?
items.back: Visibility Timeout: default 30 seconds, max 12 hours. Message Retention Period: default 4 days, min 60 seconds, max 14 days. Long Polling (ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds): max 20 seconds, which waits for messages to arrive rather than returning empty responses immediately.
items.analogy: Visibility Timeout is a 30-second lock on a trade ticket so another worker doesn't double-fill it; Long Polling is waiting 20 seconds at the dispatch window instead of polling empty 100 times a second.

items.q: In what order does the default EC2 Auto Scaling Group termination policy pick an instance to terminate?
items.back: 1) It selects the Availability Zone with the most instances to rebalance across AZs. 2) Within that AZ, it picks instances running the oldest launch template or configuration version. 3) If still tied, it terminates the instance closest to the next billing hour.
items.analogy: When Mammoth Capital scales down after market close, it trims the fullest server room first (AZ balance), retires the oldest OS build next, and keeps boxes already paid for this hour.

items.q: What is required before enabling S3 Replication (CRR/SRR), and how are existing objects replicated?
items.back: S3 Versioning must be enabled on both source and destination buckets, plus an IAM role allowing S3 to replicate. Standard CRR/SRR only replicates new objects written after turning it on; to copy objects that already existed beforehand, you must run an S3 Batch Replication job.
items.analogy: Enabling CRR turns on a live trade-blotter copier for every new trade going forward; to copy last year's archive folders too, you must kick off a separate S3 Batch Replication job.

items.q: Why do private IPv6 subnets use an Egress-Only Internet Gateway instead of a NAT Gateway?
items.back: All IPv6 addresses in AWS are publicly routable—there is no NAT for IPv6. An Egress-Only Internet Gateway is a free, stateful, horizontally scaled VPC component for IPv6 that lets instances initiate outbound traffic to the internet while blocking all unsolicited inbound IPv6 connections.
items.analogy: Since every IPv6 container gets a public street address, an Egress-Only IGW is a one-way turnstile on your homelab router—Ubuntu can pull apt updates out, but nobody on the internet can initiate in.

items.q: Network Load Balancer (NLB) vs. Application Load Balancer (ALB): when do you choose NLB?
items.back: Choose ALB (Layer 7) for HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC routing by path, host, or headers. Choose NLB (Layer 4) for raw TCP/UDP traffic, extreme throughput with ultra-low latency (millions of requests/sec), preserving client source IP natively, or when clients require a static Elastic IP per Availability Zone.
items.analogy: ALB is a reverse proxy parsing HTTP paths; NLB is Mammoth Capital's Layer-4 hardware switch blasting raw FIX protocol TCP packets to the matching engine with microsecond latency and static whitelisted IPs.

items.q: Amazon FSx for Lustre vs. Amazon EFS: when do you choose FSx for Lustre?
items.back: EFS is a managed multi-AZ NFS file system for general Linux shared directories. Choose FSx for Lustre for high-performance computing (HPC), ML training, and quantitative modeling needing sub-millisecond latencies, hundreds of GB/s throughput, Millions of IOPS, and transparent lazy-loading from S3.
items.analogy: EFS is your everyday homelab NFS share for Docker configs; FSx for Lustre is a parallel NVMe scratch array wired into Mammoth Capital's GPU cluster to chew through S3 tick archives at 100 GB/s.

items.q: Kinesis Data Streams vs. Amazon Data Firehose: how do you decide between them?
items.back: Choose Kinesis Data Streams for real-time sub-second processing, custom consumers (Lambda, Flink, EC2), multiple independent consumers, and stream replay (retention 1–365 days). Choose Data Firehose for zero-code, near-real-time (60s+ buffer) delivery straight into S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch.
items.analogy: Data Streams is Mammoth Capital's live market-data bus where execution bots read ticks in real time and replay the tape; Firehose is the automated conveyor dumping batches into S3 every minute.

items.q: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) vs. ElastiCache: when is DAX the right choice?
items.back: DAX is a fully managed, write-through in-memory cache purpose-built for DynamoDB; it uses the standard DynamoDB SDK (no application cache-invalidation code to write) and drops read latency from milliseconds to microseconds. Use ElastiCache (Redis/Memcached) for RDS/Aurora or complex custom state.
items.analogy: DAX is a drop-in CPU L1 cache wired straight into the DynamoDB client SDK; ElastiCache is a separate Redis container you explicitly code your app to check before querying Postgres.

items.q: Amazon CloudFront vs. AWS Global Accelerator: how do you choose between them?
items.back: Choose CloudFront (CDN) to cache static/dynamic HTTP/HTTPS content at hundreds of edge locations close to users. Choose Global Accelerator when you cannot cache content and need low-latency global routing over the AWS backbone for non-HTTP TCP/UDP protocols (gaming, VoIP, trading) or two static Anycast IPs.
items.analogy: CloudFront stocks copies of Mammoth Capital's research PDFs at local branch offices worldwide; Global Accelerator is a dedicated private fiber expressway routing live UDP market feeds straight to headquarters.

items.q: Compare EC2 Cluster, Spread, and Partition Placement Groups.
items.back: Cluster packs instances onto low-latency hardware in a single AZ for 10–100 Gbps HPC networking. Spread places instances on separate hardware racks (max 7 running instances per AZ per group) for critical VMs. Partition isolates large distributed clusters (HDFS, Kafka, Cassandra) across multi-instance racks.
items.analogy: Cluster puts all your trading bots in one blade chassis for microsecond hops; Spread puts each domain controller on its own breaker; Partition groups 100 Kafka nodes by rack so one rack failure stays isolated.

items.q: DynamoDB Global Secondary Index (GSI) vs. Local Secondary Index (LSI): what are the trade-offs?
items.back: An LSI uses the same partition key as the base table, must be created when the table is created, shares a 10 GB item collection limit, and supports strongly consistent reads. A GSI can use any partition/sort key, can be added or deleted anytime, has separate throughput, and is eventually consistent only.
items.analogy: An LSI is a sub-index tab bound into your ledger the day you print it; a GSI is a separate lookup book keyed on any column you add months later, updated asynchronously.

items.q: CloudFront Functions vs. Lambda@Edge: when do you choose each for edge compute?
items.back: Choose CloudFront Functions for ultra-fast (<1 ms), high-scale viewer request/response tweaks like URL rewrites, header manipulation, and JWT validation at minimal cost. Choose Lambda@Edge (Node.js/Python) when edge logic needs network/disk access, origin request triggers, or >1 ms execution time.
items.analogy: CloudFront Functions are lightweight nginx rewrite rules firing in microseconds at the front gate; Lambda@Edge is spinning up a full Python container at a regional hub to call an external API.

items.q: What network ports, protocols, and OS platforms do Amazon EFS and FSx for Windows use?
items.back: Amazon EFS speaks NFSv4 over TCP port 2049 and supports Linux instances and containers across multiple AZs (not Windows). Amazon FSx for Windows File Server speaks SMB over TCP port 445, providing native Windows NTFS permissions, Active Directory integration, and Multi-AZ DFS failover.
items.analogy: In your homelab, EFS is an /etc/exports NFSv4 mount on port 2049 for Ubuntu Docker nodes; FSx for Windows is a domain-joined SMB share on port 445 for Windows trader workstations.

items.q: When must you upgrade from EBS gp3 to io2 Block Express, and what can st1/sc1 NOT do?
items.back: Move from gp3 to io2 Block Express when a database needs more IOPS or throughput than gp3 can deliver (io2 Block Express reaches 256,000 IOPS), sub-millisecond consistency, 99.999% durability, or EBS Multi-Attach within one AZ. Throughput HDD (st1) and Cold HDD (sc1) are magnetic and cannot be boot volumes.
items.analogy: gp3 is a fast M.2 NVMe boot drive in your Ubuntu server; io2 Block Express is a dual-controller SAN volume shared by a cluster; st1/sc1 are bulk spinning hard drives you can't boot an OS from.

items.q: What is the S3 request rate limit per prefix, and how do you scale throughput past it?
items.back: Amazon S3 automatically scales to handle at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix in a bucket. To scale higher, parallelize reads and writes across multiple prefixes (e.g., 10 prefixes provide 55,000 GET/s and 35,000 PUT/s immediately).
items.analogy: One S3 prefix is a single order-book queue handling 5,500 reads/sec; sharding tick files across 10 date/symbol prefixes opens 10 parallel lanes for 55,000 reads/sec.

items.q: What are AWS Lambda's maximum execution timeout, memory allocation, and /tmp storage limits?
items.back: Max execution timeout: 15 minutes (900 seconds). Max memory: 10,240 MB (10 GB), which scales compute proportionally up to 6 vCPUs. Ephemeral /tmp storage: 512 MB default, configurable up to 10,240 MB (10 GB). Deployment package limit is 50 MB zipped (250 MB unzipped) or 10 GB container image.
items.analogy: Lambda is a sprinter with a strict 15-minute clock and a 10 GB scratchpad (/tmp); if your backtest runs for an hour or needs 500 GB of local files, move to AWS Batch or mount EFS.

items.q: What are the S3 maximum object size, single PUT limit, and Multipart Upload thresholds?
items.back: Maximum S3 object size is 5 TB. The largest file uploadable in a single PUT request is 5 GB. S3 Multipart Upload (up to 10,000 parts) is recommended for any object over 100 MB to parallelize throughput and resume failed chunks, and is mandatory for any object larger than 5 GB.
items.analogy: S3's vault holds 5-ton crates (5 TB max), but the single-PUT loading door only fits 5 GB boxes—anything larger must be split into numbered parts via Multipart Upload.

items.q: S3 Intelligent-Tiering vs. S3 Lifecycle Policies: when do you choose Intelligent-Tiering?
items.back: Use Lifecycle Policies when data cools on a predictable schedule (e.g., archive after 30 days). Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering when access patterns are unknown or shifting; for a small monthly object monitoring fee, it auto-tiers objects after 30+ days of inactivity with zero retrieval fees when accessed.
items.analogy: Lifecycle Policies are a scheduled cron job moving old logs to tape on day 30; Intelligent-Tiering is a smart tiering daemon watching which datasets quants open and demoting idle files with zero recall penalty.

items.q: DynamoDB On-Demand vs. Provisioned capacity mode: when does each minimize cost?
items.back: Choose On-Demand (pay-per-request) for unpredictable, spiky, or new workloads with low or erratic baseline traffic. Choose Provisioned capacity (paired with Auto Scaling and DynamoDB Reserved Capacity) when read/write traffic is steady and predictable, delivering substantial discounts over On-Demand.
items.analogy: On-Demand is paying per trade execution on a volatile news day; Provisioned capacity is leasing a dedicated exchange seat at a steep discount because your baseline order volume runs steady all year.

items.q: Amazon Athena vs. Amazon Redshift: when is Athena the right cost-optimized choice?
items.back: Choose Athena for serverless, ad-hoc SQL queries directly against S3 files—you pay $5 per TB scanned with zero idle compute cost (slash scan costs by 30–90% using compressed Parquet/ORC and partitioning). Choose Redshift for high-concurrency, sub-second BI dashboards and heavy daily warehouse joins.
items.analogy: Athena is querying Parquet files on your NAS with DuckDB—paying only for bytes read; Redshift is keeping a dedicated multi-node database cluster powered on 24/7 for live executive dashboards.

items.q: How does Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) cut costs when deploying third-party virtual firewalls?
items.back: Instead of running duplicate pairs of costly virtual firewall appliances in every VPC, GWLB (using GENEVE encapsulation on UDP port 6081) centralizes one auto-scaling appliance fleet in a shared inspection VPC and exposes it across accounts via Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints.
items.analogy: Instead of buying two commercial firewall appliances for every VLAN in your homelab, GWLB trunks all VPC traffic through one central inspection cluster that scales licences with actual load.

items.q: What are the minimum billable storage durations and size rules for S3 IA and Glacier tiers?
items.back: S3 Standard-IA and One Zone-IA enforce a 30-day minimum storage duration and a 128 KB minimum billable object size. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval and Glacier Flexible Retrieval enforce a 90-day minimum duration. S3 Glacier Deep Archive enforces a 180-day minimum. Deleting early still bills the full minimum.
items.analogy: Deleting a file from Glacier Deep Archive after 10 days is like breaking a 6-month office lease in week two—AWS still charges you for the full 180-day minimum commitment.

items.q: What are the retrieval times for S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval vs. Glacier Deep Archive?
items.back: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval supports Expedited (1–5 minutes), Standard (3–5 hours), and Bulk (5–12 hours, free). S3 Glacier Deep Archive does NOT support Expedited retrieval; it only offers Standard retrieval (within 12 hours) and Bulk retrieval (within 48 hours).
items.analogy: Glacier Flexible has an 'express courier' option (1–5 min Expedited); Deep Archive is locked in a remote salt mine—even standard priority takes up to 12 hours to bring up the elevator.

items.q: How do you cut Amazon EFS costs for cold files or non-critical dev/test environments?
items.back: Enable EFS Lifecycle Management to automatically move files untouched for a set window (e.g., 7–90 days) into EFS Infrequent Access (EFS IA) or EFS Archive, saving up to 90%+ on storage. For dev/test or reproducible caches that don't require multi-AZ resilience, use EFS One Zone.
items.analogy: EFS Lifecycle Management is automatically migrating stale Docker build caches from your mirrored ZFS NVMe pool down to a cheap spinning-disk tier when untouched for 30 days.

items.q: How does S3 Requester Pays cut costs when sharing massive datasets with external accounts?
items.back: Enabling S3 Requester Pays shifts the cost of S3 requests and data egress transfer to the downloading requester instead of the bucket owner (who only pays for storage). Requesters must authenticate with a valid AWS identity and include the x-amz-request-payer header; anonymous access is blocked.
items.analogy: Mammoth Capital lets partner funds download terabytes of historical market data from S3, but Requester Pays requires them to bill their own AWS account for the bandwidth.

items.q: How does AWS price data transfer for Inbound, Same-AZ, Cross-AZ, and Internet Egress traffic?
items.back: Inbound data from the internet into AWS is free. Traffic between EC2 instances in the same AZ using private IPs is free. Traffic crossing between AZs in the same Region (or using public/Elastic IPs even in the same AZ) costs per GB in both directions, and outbound internet egress carries the highest per-GB fee.
items.analogy: Packets staying on the same switch in your homelab rack (same-AZ private IP) are free; crossing town between data centers (Cross-AZ) or heading out to the ISP incurs a metered toll.

items.q: EC2 Dedicated Hosts vs. Dedicated Instances vs. Capacity Reservations: how do they differ?
items.back: Dedicated Instances run on single-tenant hardware without physical socket visibility. Dedicated Hosts expose physical sockets and cores, required for server-bound BYOL licenses (Windows Server, SQL Server, Oracle). On-Demand Capacity Reservations hold AZ capacity for any duration without a 1/3-year commitment.
items.analogy: Dedicated Instances guarantee no noisy neighbors on the host; Dedicated Hosts let you count physical CPU sockets for Oracle license auditors; Capacity Reservations just hold an empty seat at the bar.

items.q: Cost Explorer vs. AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) vs. S3 Storage Lens: what does each do?
items.back: Cost Explorer visualizes up to 13 months of historical spend and 12-month forecasts in the console. CUR exports the most granular hourly line-item billing data to S3 for Athena/QuickSight analysis. S3 Storage Lens audits organization-wide S3 usage, flagging cost waste like incomplete multipart uploads.
items.analogy: Cost Explorer is your brokerage dashboard chart; CUR is the raw tick-by-tick CSV ledger you query in Athena; S3 Storage Lens is running ncdu across every NAS bucket to spot orphaned temp chunks.
